**Surah Ta-Ha**

It is entirely Meccan, by the consensus of scholars. Regarding the occasion of revelation of (Ta-Ha), there are three opinions:

First: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to shift his weight between his two feet, standing on one foot, until this verse was revealed." This was related by [ʿAlī] (peace be upon him).

Second: "When the Qur'an was revealed to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), he and his Companions prayed and prolonged the standing. The Quraysh said: 'Allah did not send down this Qur'an to Muhammad except that he might be miserable.' So this verse was revealed." This was related by al-Ḍaḥḥāk. (p-269)

Third: Abu Jahl, al-Naḍr ibn al-Ḥārith, and al-Muṭʿim ibn ʿAdī said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "You are indeed becoming miserable by abandoning our religion." So this verse was revealed. This was related by Muqātil.

There are variant readings (qirāʾāt) of **﴿Ta-Ha﴾**:
- Ibn Kathīr and Ibn ʿĀmir read (طَه) with a fatḥa on both the ṭāʾ and the hāʾ.
- Ḥamza, al-Kisāʾī, and Abū Bakr (from ʿĀṣim) read (طِه) with a kasra on both.
- Nāfiʿ read it between the fatḥa and the kasra, nearer to the fatḥa; Khalaf reported this from al-Musayyabī.
- Abū ʿAmr read it with a fatḥa on the ṭāʾ and a kasra on the hāʾ, and ʿAbbās transmitted from him something like Ḥamza's reading.
- Ibn Masʿūd, Abū Razīn al-ʿUqaylī, Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyib, and Abū al-ʿĀliya read (طِهَ) with a kasra on the ṭāʾ and a fatḥa on the hāʾ.
- al-Ḥasan read (طَهْ) with a fatḥa on the ṭāʾ and a sukūn on the hāʾ.
- al-Ḍaḥḥāk and Muwarriq read (طِهْ) with a kasra on the ṭāʾ and a sukūn on the hāʾ.

They differed over its meaning, in four opinions:

First: its meaning is "O man." This was related by al-ʿAwfī from Ibn ʿAbbās, and al-Ḥasan, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, Mujāhid, ʿAṭāʾ, and ʿIkrima also said so. These scholars then differed over which language it belongs to, in four opinions:
- It is Nabataean. This was related by ʿIkrima from Ibn ʿAbbās, and Saʿīd ibn Jubayr said so in one report, as did al-Ḍaḥḥāk.
- It is in the dialect of ʿAkk. This was related by Abū Ṣāliḥ from Ibn ʿAbbās.
- It is Syriac. This was said by ʿIkrima in one report, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr in another, and Qatāda.
- It is Ethiopic (Ḥabashī). This was said by ʿIkrima in one report.

Ibn al-Anbārī said: "The language of the Quraysh agreed with this language in meaning."

Second: they are letters taken from names. Then there are two opinions on this:
- One: they are from the names of Allah, the Exalted. Then there are two views:
  - That the ṭāʾ is from *al-Laṭīf* (the Subtle) and the hāʾ is from *al-Hādī* (the Guide). This was said by Ibn Masʿūd and Abū al-ʿĀliya.
  - That the ṭāʾ is the beginning of His name *Ṭāhir* (the Pure) and *Ṭayyib* (the Good), and the hāʾ is the beginning of His name *Hādī* (the Guide). This was said by Saʿīd ibn Jubayr. (p-270)
- Two: they are not from the names of Allah, the Exalted. Then there are three views:
  - That the ṭāʾ is from *Ṭāba* (Ṭaba, the name of the city), which is the city of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and the hāʾ is from Makkah. This was related by Abū Sulaymān al-Dimashqī.
  - That the ṭāʾ is the joy (ṭarab) of the people of Paradise, and the hāʾ is the humiliation (hawān) of the people of the Fire.
  - That in the reckoning of *al-jumal* (the system of numerical values of letters, known as ḥisāb al-jummal), the ṭāʾ is nine and the hāʾ is five, making fourteen. The meaning is: "O full moon (al-badr), We did not send down the Qur'an to you so that you would be miserable." al-Thaʿlabī related both opinions.

Third: it is an oath that Allah swore by, and it is among His names. This was related by ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭalḥa from Ibn ʿAbbās. We have explained the meaning of it being a name at the opening of (Maryam). al-Quraẓī said: Allah swore by His length (ṭawl) and His guidance (hidāya). This opinion is close in meaning to the one before it.

Fourth: its meaning is "Tread the earth with your two feet." This was said by Muqātil ibn Ḥayyān.

The meaning of His words **﴿to be miserable﴾**: that you would exert yourself and reach the extent of hardship that you have reached. This is because he strove hard in worship and went to excess, to the point that he used to shift his weight between his feet because of the length of the standing. So he was commanded to lighten it.

His words, Exalted is He: **﴿Only as a reminder﴾**. al-Akhfash said: it is an apposition (badal) for His words **﴿to be miserable﴾**, meaning: We did not send it down except as a reminder, that is, an admonition.

His words, Exalted is He: **﴿A revelation﴾**. al-Zajjāj said: the meaning is: We sent it down as a revelation (tanzīlan). **﴿The heights﴾** is the plural of *al-ʿulyā* (the highest). You say: a high sky (samāʾ ʿulyā) and high heavens (samāwāt ʿulan), like *al-kubrā* (the greatest) and *al-kubar*. As for **﴿the earth beneath﴾** (al-thará), it is the moist soil. The commentators say that what is intended is the moist soil beneath the seventh earth.

His words, Exalted is He: **﴿And if you speak aloud﴾**, that is, if you raise your voice, **﴿then indeed He knows the secret﴾**. The meaning is: do not strain yourself by raising your voice, for Allah knows the secret.

Regarding what is meant by **﴿the secret and what is more hidden﴾** there are five opinions:

First: the secret is what a person keeps within himself, and what is more hidden is what has not yet occurred but will occur. This was related by a group of scholars from Ibn ʿAbbās, and al-Ḍaḥḥāk said so.

Second: the secret is what you speak to yourself about, and what is more hidden is what you have not uttered. This was said by Saʿīd ibn Jubayr.

Third: the secret is the deed that a person conceals from people, and what is more hidden than it is the whisper (waswasa). This was said by Mujāhid.

Fourth: the meaning of the statement is: He knows the secret conversations of His servants, and He has concealed His own secret from them so that it is not known. This was said by Zayd ibn Aslam and his son.

Fifth: He knows what a person has confided to another and what he has hidden within himself. This was said by al-Farrāʾ.

His words, Exalted is He: **﴿To Him belong the most beautiful names﴾**. We have explained this in (al-Aʿrāf: 180).

- al-Ḍaḥḥāk and Muwarriq read (طِهْ) with a kasra on the ṭāʾ and a sukūn on the hāʾ.

They differed over its meaning, in four opinions:

First: its meaning is "O man." This was related by al-ʿAwfī from Ibn ʿAbbās, and al-Ḥasan, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, Mujāhid, ʿAṭāʾ, and ʿIkrima also said so. These scholars then differed over which language it belongs to, in four opinions:
- It is Nabataean. This was related by ʿIkrima from Ibn ʿAbbās, and Saʿīd ibn Jubayr said so in one report, as did al-Ḍaḥḥāk.
- It is in the dialect of ʿAkk. This was related by Abū Ṣāliḥ from Ibn ʿAbbās.
- It is Syriac. This was said by ʿIkrima in one report, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr in another, and Qatāda.
- It is Ethiopic (Ḥabashī). This was said by ʿIkrima in one report.

Ibn al-Anbārī said: "The language of the Quraysh agreed with this language in meaning."

Second: they are letters taken from names. Then there are two opinions on this:
- One: they are from the names of Allah, the Exalted. Then there are two views:
  - That the ṭāʾ is from *al-Laṭīf* (the Subtle) and the hāʾ is from *al-Hādī* (the Guide). This was said by Ibn Masʿūd and Abū al-ʿĀliya.
  - That the ṭāʾ is the beginning of His name *Ṭāhir* (the Pure) and *Ṭayyib* (the Good), and the hāʾ is the beginning of His name *Hādī* (the Guide). This was said by Saʿīd ibn Jubayr. (p-270)
- Two: they are not from the names of Allah, the Exalted. Then there are three views:
  - That the ṭāʾ is from *Ṭāba* (Ṭaba, the name of the city), which is the city of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and the hāʾ is from Makkah. This was related by Abū Sulaymān al-Dimashqī.
  - That the ṭāʾ is the joy (ṭarab) of the people of Paradise, and the hāʾ is the humiliation (hawān) of the people of the Fire.
  - That in the reckoning of *al-jumal* (the system of numerical values of letters, known as ḥisāb al-jummal), the ṭāʾ is nine and the hāʾ is five, making fourteen. Third: it is an oath that Allah swore by, and it is among His names. This was related by ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭalḥa from Ibn ʿAbbās. We have explained the meaning of it being a name at the opening of (Maryam). al-Quraẓī said: Allah swore by His length (ṭawl) and His guidance (hidāya). This opinion is close in meaning to the one before it.

Fourth: its meaning is "Tread the earth with your two feet." This was said by Muqātil ibn Ḥayyān.

The meaning of His words **﴿to be miserable﴾**: that you would exert yourself and reach the extent of hardship that you have reached. This is because he strove hard in worship and went to excess, to the point that he used to shift his weight between his feet because of the length of the standing. So he was commanded to lighten it.

His words, Exalted is He: **﴿Only as a reminder﴾**. al-Akhfash said: it is an apposition (badal) for His words **﴿to be miserable﴾**, meaning: We did not send it down except as a reminder, that is, an admonition.

His words, Exalted is He: **﴿A revelation﴾**. al-Zajjāj said: the meaning is: We sent it down as a revelation (tanzīlan). **﴿The heights﴾** is the plural of *al-ʿulyā* (the highest). You say: a high sky (samāʾ ʿulyā) and high heavens (samāwāt ʿulan), like *al-kubrā* (the greatest) and *al-kubar*. As for **﴿the earth beneath﴾** (al-thará), it is the moist soil. The commentators say that what is intended is the moist soil beneath the seventh earth.

His words, Exalted is He: **﴿And if you speak aloud﴾**, that is, if you raise your voice, **﴿then indeed He knows the secret﴾**. The meaning is: do not strain yourself by raising your voice, for Allah knows the secret.

Regarding what is meant by **﴿the secret and what is more hidden﴾** there are five opinions:

First: the secret is what a person keeps within himself, and what is more hidden is what has not yet occurred but will occur. This was related by a group of scholars from Ibn ʿAbbās, and al-Ḍaḥḥāk said so.

Second: the secret is what you speak to yourself about, and what is more hidden is what you have not uttered. This was said by Saʿīd ibn Jubayr.

Third: the secret is the deed that a person conceals from people, and what is more hidden than it is the whisper (waswasa). This was said by Mujāhid.

Fourth: the meaning of the statement is: He knows the secret conversations of His servants, and He has concealed His own secret from them so that it is not known. This was said by Zayd ibn Aslam and his son.

Fifth: He knows what a person has confided to another and what he has hidden within himself. This was said by al-Farrāʾ.

His words, Exalted is He: **﴿To Him belong the most beautiful names﴾**. We have explained this in (al-Aʿrāf: 180).

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 20, verse 9–16:

The words of the Exalted: ﴿Has the story of Moses reached you?﴾ This is an interrogative of affirmation (istifham taqrir), and its meaning is: it has indeed reached you. Ibn al-Anbari said: It is well known among the linguists that "hal" (هَلْ) comes to express the meaning of "qad" (قَدْ), for the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, who was the most eloquent of the Arabs, said: "O Allah, have I not (hal) conveyed?" meaning: "Indeed I have conveyed."

Wahb ibn Munabbih said: Moses asked Shu'ayb, peace be upon them both, for permission to return to his mother, and he granted it. So he set out with his family, and a child was born to him on the way, on a wintry night. He struck (flint) but the spark would not catch. While he was busy with that, he saw a fire from afar on the left side of the road. We have mentioned this narration in full in the book "al-Hada'iq," but we disliked lengthening the tafsir with stories, since our aim is to be brief in the tafsir so that it may be easy to memorize. The exegetes said: He saw a light, but he (the narrator) reported what was in Moses' thinking.

﴿So he said to his family﴾, meaning: his wife, ﴿Wait﴾; that is: stay where you are. Hamzah read: (لِأَهْلِهُ امْكُثُوا) with a dammah on the ha' here and in (al-Qasas: 29). ﴿Indeed I have perceived a fire﴾. Al-Farra' said: "Innī ānastu" means "innī wajadtu" (I have found); it is said: "Hal ānasta aḥadan?" meaning: did you find anyone? Ibn Qutaybah said: "ānastu" means "I saw" (abṣartu). As for the qabas (a brand), al-Zajjaj said: it is what you take from the fire at the head of a stick, or at the head of a wick.

The words of the Exalted: ﴿Or I may find at the fire guidance﴾. Al-Farra' said: He meant: a guide (hādiyan), and he expressed it in the form of a verbal noun (maṣdar). Ibn al-Anbari said: "ʿalā" here may be taken to mean "ʿinda" (at), and to mean "maʿa" (with), and to mean the particle "bi" (with). The exegetes mention that he had lost the way, so he knew that a fire must have a kindler. Al-Zajjaj related that he had lost the water, so he hoped to find someone who would guide him to the road or show him the water.

The words of the Exalted: ﴿So when he came to it﴾, meaning: the fire, ﴿he was called: "O Moses! Indeed, I am your Lord"﴾. He repeated the pronoun only to emphasize the indication, to establish knowledge, and to remove doubt; similar to it is: ﴿Indeed I am the clear warner﴾ [al-Hijr: 89]. Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and Abu Ja'far read: (أَنِّي) with a fatha on the alif and the ya'. Nafi', ʿĀṣim, Ibn ʿĀmir, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read: (إِنِّي) with a kasra on the alif, except that Nafi' opened the ya'. Al-Zajjaj said: Whoever reads "annī anā" with a fatha, the meaning is: he was called [that I am your Lord]; and whoever reads with a kasra, the meaning is: he was called, "O Moses," and Allah said: "Indeed I am your Lord."

The words of the Exalted: ﴿So take off your sandals﴾. Concerning the reason for His command to remove them there are two sayings:

One: they were made of the skin of a dead donkey. This was related by Ibn Mas'ud from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and ʿAlī ibn Abi Talib, may Allah ennoble his face, and ʿIkrimah said likewise.

The second: they were made of the skin of a slaughtered cow, but he was commanded to remove them so that he would touch the dust of the sacred land, and so its blessing would reach him. This was said by al-Hasan, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Mujahid and Qatadah.

The words of the Exalted: ﴿Indeed you are in the sacred valley﴾. There are two sayings concerning it, which we have mentioned in (al-Ma'idah: 21) at His words: ﴿the sacred land﴾.

The words of the Exalted: ﴿Tuwan﴾. Ibn Kathir, Nafi' and Abu 'Amr read: (طُوى وَأَنَا) without tanwin. ʿĀṣim, Ibn ʿĀmir, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read: (طُوًى) with tanwin, and all of them put a dammah on the ta'. al-Hasan and Abu Haywah read: (طِوًى) with a kasra on the ta' with tanwin. ʿAlī ibn Nasr from Abu ʿAmr read: (طِوى) with a kasra on the ta' without tanwin. Al-Zajjaj said that regarding "Tuwan" there are four aspects: (طُوًى) with a dammah on its first letter, with and without tanwin. Whoever puts tanwin on it, it is a noun for the valley, and it is masculine, named with a masculine on the pattern fu'al, like ḥuṭam and ṣurad. Whoever does not put tanwin leaves it uninflected for two reasons:

One: that it is derived from a word (ṭāwin) so that it becomes like ʿUmar, which is derived from ʿĀmir, so it is not inflected, just as ʿUmar is not inflected.

The second reason: that it is a name for the place, as in His words: ﴿in the blessed place﴾ [al-Qasas: 30]. When it is read with a kasra and tanwin, it is like mi'an, and the meaning is: sanctified time after time, as ʿAdi ibn Zayd said:

"O blamer, indeed blame in other than its proper place is upon me, a repeated tuwan of your going astray."

That is: repeated blame upon me. Whoever does not put tanwin makes it a name for the place.

[The exegetes have three sayings on the meaning of "Tuwa":

One: that it is the name of the valley; related by Ibn Abi Talhah from Ibn ʿAbbas.

The second: that the meaning of "tuwan" is: "trample the valley," related by ʿIkrimah from Ibn ʿAbbas, and from Mujahid as two sayings.

The third: that it was sanctified twice; said by al-Hasan and Qatadah.]

The words of the Exalted: ﴿And I have chosen you﴾, that is: I have selected you. Hamzah and al-Mufaddal read: (وَأَنَّا) with a doubled nun, (اخْتَرْنَاكَ) with an alif. ﴿So listen to what is revealed﴾; that is: to that which is revealed. Ibn al-Anbari said: "listening" here is to be understood as attentive silence; the meaning: be silent for My revelation. The revelation here is His words: ﴿Indeed I am Allah; there is no deity except Me, so worship Me﴾; that is: affirm My oneness, ﴿and establish prayer for My remembrance﴾. There are two sayings concerning it:

One: establish the prayer whenever you remember that a prayer is due upon you, whether you are within its time or not; this is the saying of the majority. Anas related from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "Whoever forgets a prayer, let him pray it when he remembers it; there is no expiation for it other than that," and he recited: "establish the prayer for My remembrance."

The second: establish the prayer so that you remember Me in it; said by Mujahid. It was also said that the speech is connected to His words: ﴿so listen﴾, so the meaning is: listen to what is revealed and listen to My remembrance. Ibn Mas'ud, Ubayy ibn Ka'b and Ibn al-Sumayfa' read: (وَأَقِمِ الصَّلَاةَ لِلذِّكْرَى) with two lams and a shaddah on the dhal.

The words of the Exalted: ﴿I almost conceal it﴾. Most readers put a dammah on the alif.

Then, regarding the meaning of the statement, there are three sayings:

One: "I almost conceal it from myself." This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Mujahid and others. Ibn Mas'ud, Ubayy ibn Ka'b and Muhammad ibn ʿAli read: (أَكَادُ أُخْفِيهَا مِن نَفْسِي). Al-Farra' said: the meaning is: how then should I make it apparent to you? Al-Mubarrad said: This is according to the custom of the Arabs; when they exaggerate in concealing something, they say: "I concealed it even from myself," that is: I did not inform anyone of it.

The second: the sentence is complete at His words: ﴿I almost﴾, and after it there is an implied element, its estimate being: "I almost bring it," and the beginning is: "I conceal it." Dhabi' al-Burjumi said:

"I intended but did not do; I almost did, and I wish that Uthman's wives had been left weeping over him."

He meant: I almost did.

The third: that the meaning of "akadu" is: "uridu" (I want). A poet said:

"She wanted and I wanted, and that is the best of wishes, if only what has passed of the sport of passion would return."

Its meaning: she wanted and I wanted. Ibn al-Anbari mentioned both.

If it is said: what is the benefit of this intense concealment?

The answer: it is for warning and fear, for whoever does not know when his enemy will attack is more cautious. Sa'id ibn Jubayr, ʿUrwah ibn al-Zubayr, Abu Raja' al-ʿUtaridi and Humayd ibn Qays read: (أُخْفِيهَا) with a fatha on the alif. Al-Zajjaj said: its meaning is: "I almost make it apparent." Imru' al-Qays said:

"If you bury the disease, we will not conceal it; and if you raise war, we will not sit idle."

That is: if you bury the disease, we will not make it apparent. He said: this reading is clearer in meaning, because the meaning of "akadu uzhiruha" (I almost reveal it) is: I have concealed it and I almost reveal it. ﴿So that every soul may be recompensed for what it strives﴾; that is: for what it does. The phrase ﴿so that﴾ is connected to His words: "Indeed the Hour is coming," so that it may be recompensed. It is also permissible that it is connected to "Establish the prayer for My remembrance," so that it may be recompensed.

The words of the Exalted: ﴿So let not one who does not believe in it avert you from it﴾; that is: from belief in it. ﴿Him who does not believe in it﴾, that is: whoever does not believe in its occurrence. The address to the Prophet ﷺ is an address to all of his community. ﴿And follows his desire﴾; that is: his inclination, and opposes the command of Allah, Mighty and Majestic. ﴿And thus perish﴾; that is: and so be destroyed. Al-Zajjaj said: it is said: "radiya yardā" when one perishes.

We have mentioned this narration in full in the book "al-Hada'iq," but we disliked lengthening the tafsir with stories, since our aim is to be brief in the tafsir so that it may be easy to memorize. The exegetes said: He saw a light, but he (the narrator) reported what was in Moses' thinking.

﴿So he said to his family﴾, meaning: his wife, ﴿Wait﴾; that is: stay where you are. Hamzah read: (لِأَهْلِهُ امْكُثُوا) with a dammah on the ha' here and in (al-Qasas: 29). ﴿Indeed I have perceived a fire﴾. Al-Farra' said: "Innī ānastu" means "innī wajadtu" (I have found); it is said: "Hal ānasta aḥadan?" meaning: did you find anyone? Ibn Qutaybah said: "ānastu" means "I saw" (abṣartu). As for the qabas (a brand), al-Zajjaj said: it is what you take from the fire at the head of a stick, or at the head of a wick.

The words of the Exalted: ﴿Or I may find at the fire guidance﴾. Al-Farra' said: He meant: a guide (hādiyan), and he expressed it in the form of a verbal noun (maṣdar). Ibn al-Anbari said: "ʿalā" here may be taken to mean "ʿinda" (at), and to mean "maʿa" (with), and to mean the particle "bi" (with). The exegetes mention that he had lost the way, so he knew that a fire must have a kindler. Al-Zajjaj related that he had lost the water, so he hoped to find someone who would guide him to the road or show him the water.

The words of the Exalted: ﴿So when he came to it﴾, meaning: the fire, ﴿he was called: "O Moses! Indeed, I am your Lord"﴾. He repeated the pronoun only to emphasize the indication, to establish knowledge, and to remove doubt; similar to it is: ﴿Indeed I am the clear warner﴾ [al-Hijr: 89]. Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and Abu Ja'far read: (أَنِّي) with a fatha on the alif and the ya'. Nafi', ʿĀṣim, Ibn ʿĀmir, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read: (إِنِّي) with a kasra on the alif, except that Nafi' opened the ya'. Al-Zajjaj said: Whoever reads "annī anā" with a fatha, the meaning is: he was called [that I am your Lord]; and whoever reads with a kasra, the meaning is: he was called, "O Moses," and Allah said: "Indeed I am your Lord."

The words of the Exalted: ﴿So take off your sandals﴾. Concerning the reason for His command to remove them there are two sayings:

One: they were made of the skin of a dead donkey. This was related by Ibn Mas'ud from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and ʿAlī ibn Abi Talib, may Allah ennoble his face, and ʿIkrimah said likewise.

The second: they were made of the skin of a slaughtered cow, but he was commanded to remove them so that he would touch the dust of the sacred land, and so its blessing would reach him. This was said by al-Hasan, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Mujahid and Qatadah.

The words of the Exalted: ﴿Indeed you are in the sacred valley﴾. There are two sayings concerning it, which we have mentioned in (al-Ma'idah: 21) at His words: ﴿the sacred land﴾.

The words of the Exalted: ﴿Tuwan﴾. Ibn Kathir, Nafi' and Abu 'Amr read: (طُوى وَأَنَا) without tanwin. ʿĀṣim, Ibn ʿĀmir, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read: (طُوًى) with tanwin, and all of them put a dammah on the ta'. al-Hasan and Abu Haywah read: (طِوًى) with a kasra on the ta' with tanwin. ʿAlī ibn Nasr from Abu ʿAmr read: (طِوى) with a kasra on the ta' without tanwin. Al-Zajjaj said that regarding "Tuwan" there are four aspects: (طُوًى) with a dammah on its first letter, with and without tanwin. Whoever puts tanwin on it, it is a noun for the valley, and it is masculine, named with a masculine on the pattern fu'al, like ḥuṭam and ṣurad. Whoever does not put tanwin leaves it uninflected for two reasons:

One: that it is derived from a word (ṭāwin) so that it becomes like ʿUmar, which is derived from ʿĀmir, so it is not inflected, just as ʿUmar is not inflected.

The second reason: that it is a name for the place, as in His words: ﴿in the blessed place﴾ [al-Qasas: 30]. When it is read with a kasra and tanwin, it is like mi'an, and the meaning is: sanctified time after time, as ʿAdi ibn Zayd said:

"O blamer, indeed blame in other than its proper place is upon me, a repeated tuwan of your going astray."

That is: repeated blame upon me. Whoever does not put tanwin makes it a name for the place.

[The exegetes have three sayings on the meaning of "Tuwa":

One: that it is the name of the valley; related by Ibn Abi Talhah from Ibn ʿAbbas.

The second: that the meaning of "tuwan" is: "trample the valley," related by ʿIkrimah from Ibn ʿAbbas, and from Mujahid as two sayings.

The third: that it was sanctified twice; said by al-Hasan and Qatadah.]

The words of the Exalted: ﴿And I have chosen you﴾, that is: I have selected you. Hamzah and al-Mufaddal read: (وَأَنَّا) with a doubled nun, (اخْتَرْنَاكَ) with an alif. ﴿So listen to what is revealed﴾; that is: to that which is revealed. Ibn al-Anbari said: "listening" here is to be understood as attentive silence; the meaning: be silent for My revelation. The revelation here is His words: ﴿Indeed I am Allah; there is no deity except Me, so worship Me﴾; that is: affirm My oneness, ﴿and establish prayer for My remembrance﴾. There are two sayings concerning it:

One: establish the prayer whenever you remember that a prayer is due upon you, whether you are within its time or not; this is the saying of the majority. Anas related from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "Whoever forgets a prayer, let him pray it when he remembers it; there is no expiation for it other than that," and he recited: "establish the prayer for My remembrance."

The second: establish the prayer so that you remember Me in it; said by Mujahid. It was also said that the speech is connected to His words: ﴿so listen﴾, so the meaning is: listen to what is revealed and listen to My remembrance. Ibn Mas'ud, Ubayy ibn Ka'b and Ibn al-Sumayfa' read: (وَأَقِمِ الصَّلَاةَ لِلذِّكْرَى) with two lams and a shaddah on the dhal.

The words of the Exalted: ﴿I almost conceal it﴾. Most readers put a dammah on the alif.

Then, regarding the meaning of the statement, there are three sayings:

One: "I almost conceal it from myself." This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Mujahid and others. Ibn Mas'ud, Ubayy ibn Ka'b and Muhammad ibn ʿAli read: (أَكَادُ أُخْفِيهَا مِن نَفْسِي). Al-Farra' said: the meaning is: how then should I make it apparent to you? Al-Mubarrad said: This is according to the custom of the Arabs; when they exaggerate in concealing something, they say: "I concealed it even from myself," that is: I did not inform anyone of it.

The second: the sentence is complete at His words: ﴿I almost﴾, and after it there is an implied element, its estimate being: "I almost bring it," and the beginning is: "I conceal it." Dhabi' al-Burjumi said:

"I intended but did not do; I almost did, and I wish that Uthman's wives had been left weeping over him."

He meant: I almost did.

The third: that the meaning of "akadu" is: "uridu" (I want). A poet said:

"She wanted and I wanted, and that is the best of wishes, if only what has passed of the sport of passion would return."

Its meaning: she wanted and I wanted. Ibn al-Anbari mentioned both.

If it is said: what is the benefit of this intense concealment?

The answer: it is for warning and fear, for whoever does not know when his enemy will attack is more cautious. Sa'id ibn Jubayr, ʿUrwah ibn al-Zubayr, Abu Raja' al-ʿUtaridi and Humayd ibn Qays read: (أُخْفِيهَا) with a fatha on the alif. Al-Zajjaj said: its meaning is: "I almost make it apparent." Imru' al-Qays said:

"If you bury the disease, we will not conceal it; and if you raise war, we will not sit idle."

That is: if you bury the disease, we will not make it apparent. He said: this reading is clearer in meaning, because the meaning of "akadu uzhiruha" (I almost reveal it) is: I have concealed it and I almost reveal it. ﴿So that every soul may be recompensed for what it strives﴾; that is: for what it does. The phrase ﴿so that﴾ is connected to His words: "Indeed the Hour is coming," so that it may be recompensed. It is also permissible that it is connected to "Establish the prayer for My remembrance," so that it may be recompensed.

The words of the Exalted: ﴿So let not one who does not believe in it avert you from it﴾; that is: from belief in it. ﴿Him who does not believe in it﴾, that is: whoever does not believe in its occurrence. The address to the Prophet ﷺ is an address to all of his community. ﴿And follows his desire﴾; that is: his inclination, and opposes the command of Allah, Mighty and Majestic. ﴿And thus perish﴾; that is: and so be destroyed. Al-Zajjaj said: it is said: "radiya yardā" when one perishes.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 20, verse 17–23:

His words, exalted is He: ﴿And what is that in your right hand?﴾ Al-Zajjaj said: "Tilka" (that) is a demonstrative noun functioning in the sense of "allati" (the one which), and the meaning is: "What is the one in your right hand?"

His words, exalted is He: ﴿I lean upon it﴾. Al-tawakku' (leaning) is putting one's weight upon something. ﴿And I beat down (leaves) with it﴾. Al-Farra' said: I strike the dry trees with it so that their leaves fall, and then my sheep graze on them. Al-Zajjaj said: Its derivation is from "anni uhilu al-shay'a ila al-hashashah wa al-imkan" (I turn a thing to softness and possibility). Al-Ma'arib (needs/purposes) are the needs; its singular is ma'aribah and ma'urbah. Qutaybah and Warsh related "ma'arib" with imalat al-hamzah (inclination of the hamzah). (p-278)

If it is said: What is the benefit of Allah, exalted is He, asking him: ﴿And what is that in your right hand?﴾ when He knows? Concerning this there are two answers:

The first: its wording is the wording of a question and its course is the course of a question, so that the addressee answers by acknowledging it, and the proof is thereby established against him through his confession, so he cannot deny it. A similar example in speech is that you say to someone you are addressing, while you have water with you: "What is this?" He says: "Water." Then you apply some dye to it, and if he says: "It has always been like this," you say to him: "Did you not admit that it is water?" and thus you establish the proof against him. This is the statement of al-Zajjaj. According to this, the benefit is that He confirmed to Musa that it was a staff, when He wished to show him His power in turning it into a serpent, so the miracle occurred with it after the certainty regarding its matter.

The second: that when Allah, exalted is He, perceived what was in Musa's heart of awe and reverence at the time of speaking, He wished to make him at ease and lighten the weight of the fear he was in, so He made this speech for the sake of putting him at ease. This was related by Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi.

If it is said: It would have sufficed in the answer for him to say: ﴿It is my staff﴾, so what is the benefit in his saying: ﴿I lean upon it﴾ to the end of the speech, when it is only explained to one who does not know its benefits? Concerning this there are three answers:

The first: he answered with his saying: ﴿It is my staff﴾, then he was asked: "What do you do with it?" and he mentioned the rest of the speech as an answer to a second question. This was said by Ibn Abbas and Wahb.

The second: he only showed its benefits and explained his need for it, out of fear that He would command him to cast it down like the two sandals. This was said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr.

The third: he explained its benefits so that he would not be seen as carrying it in vain. This was said by al-Mawardi.

If it is said: Why did he limit himself to mentioning some of its benefits and not lengthen the explanation? Concerning this there are [three] answers: (p-279)

The first: he disliked to be occupied away from the speech of Allah by enumerating its benefits.

The second: he was content with the knowledge of Allah concerning them, dispensing with a lengthy enumeration.

The third: he limited himself to the necessary benefits rather than the incidental ones.

It was said: it used to shine for him at night, repel the vermin from him, and bear fruit for him whenever he desired fruits. Concerning its kind there are two statements:

The first: that it was of the myrtle of Paradise. This was said by Ibn Abbas. The second: that it was of the thorny-bush (awsaj).

If it is said: "Al-ma'arib" is plural, so how did He say: ﴿other﴾, and not say: "ukhar" (others, plural)?

The answer: that al-ma'arib carries the meaning of a group, so it is as if He said: a group of needs, other ones. This was said by al-Zajjaj.

His words, exalted is He: ﴿He said: Cast it down, O Musa﴾. The exegetes said: He cast it down thinking that he had been commanded to abandon it, then he heard a sound and turned, and behold, it was like the greatest serpent, passing over a great rock and swallowing it, so he fled from it.

Concerning the purpose of displaying this sign on the night of the address there are two statements:

The first: so that he would not fear it when he cast it down before Pharaoh.

The second: so that He would show him that the One to whom I send you is other than what I showed you; just as I subdued for you the greatest, which is the serpent, I will subdue for you the lesser. (p-280)

Then Allah, exalted is He, commanded him to take it while it was still in its form as a serpent, so he placed his hand upon it and it returned to a staff. This is His saying: ﴿We will return it to its former form﴾. Al-Farra' said: its way (tariqah); he says: We will return it to a staff as it was. Al-Zajjaj said: ﴿Sirataha﴾ is in the accusative by the removal of the preposition and the verb reaching it; the meaning is: We will return it to its form.

If it is said: The staff was only one and its casting was once, so what is the reason for the differing reports about it? For He says in (al-A'raf 107): ﴿then behold, it was a manifest serpent﴾, and here: ﴿a serpent﴾, and in another place: ﴿as if it were a jann﴾ [al-Naml: 10], and the jann is not great, while the thu'ban is the greatest of serpents?

The answer: its description as a jann is an expression of the beginning of its state, and its description as a thu'ban is a report of the end of its state. The word "hayyah" (serpent) applies to the small and the large, the male and the female. Al-Zajjaj said: its creation was the nature of a great serpent, and its quivering, its movement, and its agility were like the quivering and agility of the jann.

His words, exalted is He: ﴿And draw your hand to your side (janah)﴾. Al-Farra' said: al-janah is from the lower part of the upper arm to the armpit.

Abu Ubaydah said: al-janah is the side of the body, and he recited:

﴿I press it to the chest and the side﴾

His words, exalted is He: ﴿It will come forth white, without harm﴾; that is, without leprosy. ﴿As another sign﴾; that is, a proof of your truthfulness besides the staff. Al-Zajjaj said: the accusative of "ayatan" is according to the meaning: We have given you a sign, or We will give you [a sign].

His words, exalted is He: ﴿That We may show you of Our greatest signs.﴾

If it is said: Why did He not say: "al-kubar" (the greatest, plural)? Concerning this there are three answers:

The first: it is like His saying: ﴿other needs﴾, which we have explained. This is the statement of al-Farra'.

The second: that there is an ellipsis in it, its estimate being: that We may show you of Our signs the greatest sign. Abu Ubaydah said: there is an inversion in it, its estimate being: that We may show you the greatest of Our signs.

The third: that this was only for the agreement of the verse-endings (ra's al-ayy). Al-Tha'labi related both statements.

The third: he explained its benefits so that he would not be seen as carrying it in vain. This was said by al-Mawardi.

If it is said: Why did he limit himself to mentioning some of its benefits and not lengthen the explanation? Concerning this there are [three] answers: (p-279)

The first: he disliked to be occupied away from the speech of Allah by enumerating its benefits.

The second: he was content with the knowledge of Allah concerning them, dispensing with a lengthy enumeration.

The third: he limited himself to the necessary benefits rather than the incidental ones.

It was said: it used to shine for him at night, repel the vermin from him, and bear fruit for him whenever he desired fruits. Concerning its kind there are two statements:

The first: that it was of the myrtle of Paradise. This was said by Ibn Abbas. The second: that it was of the thorny-bush (awsaj).

If it is said: "Al-ma'arib" is plural, so how did He say: ﴿other﴾, and not say: "ukhar" (others, plural)?

The answer: that al-ma'arib carries the meaning of a group, so it is as if He said: a group of needs, other ones. This was said by al-Zajjaj.

His words, exalted is He: ﴿He said: Cast it down, O Musa﴾. The exegetes said: He cast it down thinking that he had been commanded to abandon it, then he heard a sound and turned, and behold, it was like the greatest serpent, passing over a great rock and swallowing it, so he fled from it.

Concerning the purpose of displaying this sign on the night of the address there are two statements:

The first: so that he would not fear it when he cast it down before Pharaoh.

The second: so that He would show him that the One to whom I send you is other than what I showed you; just as I subdued for you the greatest, which is the serpent, I will subdue for you the lesser. (p-280)

Then Allah, exalted is He, commanded him to take it while it was still in its form as a serpent, so he placed his hand upon it and it returned to a staff. This is His saying: ﴿We will return it to its former form﴾. Al-Farra' said: its way (tariqah); he says: We will return it to a staff as it was. Al-Zajjaj said: ﴿Sirataha﴾ is in the accusative by the removal of the preposition and the verb reaching it; the meaning is: We will return it to its form.

If it is said: The staff was only one and its casting was once, so what is the reason for the differing reports about it? For He says in (al-A'raf 107): ﴿then behold, it was a manifest serpent﴾, and here: ﴿a serpent﴾, and in another place: ﴿as if it were a jann﴾ [al-Naml: 10], and the jann is not great, while the thu'ban is the greatest of serpents?

The answer: its description as a jann is an expression of the beginning of its state, and its description as a thu'ban is a report of the end of its state. The word "hayyah" (serpent) applies to the small and the large, the male and the female. Al-Zajjaj said: its creation was the nature of a great serpent, and its quivering, its movement, and its agility were like the quivering and agility of the jann.

His words, exalted is He: ﴿And draw your hand to your side (janah)﴾. Al-Farra' said: al-janah is from the lower part of the upper arm to the armpit.

Abu Ubaydah said: al-janah is the side of the body, and he recited:

﴿I press it to the chest and the side﴾

His words, exalted is He: ﴿It will come forth white, without harm﴾; that is, without leprosy. ﴿As another sign﴾; that is, a proof of your truthfulness besides the staff. Al-Zajjaj said: the accusative of "ayatan" is according to the meaning: We have given you a sign, or We will give you [a sign].

His words, exalted is He: ﴿That We may show you of Our greatest signs.﴾

If it is said: Why did He not say: "al-kubar" (the greatest, plural)? Concerning this there are three answers:

The first: it is like His saying: ﴿other needs﴾, which we have explained. This is the statement of al-Farra'.

The second: that there is an ellipsis in it, its estimate being: that We may show you of Our signs the greatest sign. Abu Ubaydah said: there is an inversion in it, its estimate being: that We may show you the greatest of Our signs.

The third: that this was only for the agreement of the verse-endings (ra's al-ayy). Al-Tha'labi related both statements.

**Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on Surah 20, verses 24–35:**

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, he has transgressed﴾; that is, he exceeded the limit in disobedience.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Expand for me my breast﴾. The mufassirun (commentators on the Qur'an) said: Musa's breast constricted at what he had been charged with, namely confronting Fir'awn and his troops, so he asked Allah, Exalted is He, to widen his heart toward the truth so that he would not fear Fir'awn and his troops. The meaning of His saying, ﴿and ease my task for me﴾, is: make easy for me what You have sent me to do. ﴿And loosen a knot from my tongue﴾. Ibn Qutaybah said: there was a speech impediment (rutta) in him. The mufassirun said: Fir'awn had placed Musa in his lap when he was a child, and Musa took hold of Fir'awn's beard with his hand and pulled it, so Fir'awn intended to kill him. Asiya said to him: "Indeed, he does not understand. I will show you the proof of that: place before him two embers and two pearls. If he avoids the two embers, you will know that he understands." Musa took an ember and placed it in his mouth, and it burned his tongue and a knot formed in it. So he asked for its knot to be loosened, so that they would understand his speech.

As for the wazir (minister), Ibn Qutaybah said: the origin of wizara is from wizr, which means burden, because the wazir bears the weight on behalf of the ruler. Al-Zajjaj said: its derivation is from wizr, and the wizr is the mountain to which one clings in order to be saved from destruction; likewise the wazir of the caliph means the one on whom he relies in his affairs and to whose opinion he resorts. The word ﴿Harun﴾ is in the accusative for two reasons. The first: that "ijʿal" (make) takes two objects, so the meaning is: make Harun, my brother, my wazir, and thus "waziran" is the second object. It is also possible that ﴿Harun﴾ is a substitute (badal) for ﴿a wazir﴾, so the meaning is: make for me a wazir from my family, then Harun is substituted for wazir; the first is better. Al-Mawardi said: Musa only asked Allah, Exalted is He, to make for him a wazir because he did not want to be restricted to the role of a minister, so that he might be a partner in prophethood; otherwise it would have been permissible for him to be appointed as a minister without asking. Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read "akhi" (my brother) with a fatha on the ya' (ya' of akhi).

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Strengthen my back through him﴾. Al-Farra' said: this is a supplication from Musa, and the meaning is: strengthen my back through him, O my Lord, and make him a partner with me, O my Lord, in my affair. Ibn 'Amir read "ashdud" with an alif that is cut off and fatha, and "ushrik-hu" with a damma on the alif, and so he begins with the two alifs. Abu 'Ali said: this recitation (qira'ah) is in the form of a response and a conditional, but the more apparent reading is supplication rather than report, because what precedes it is a supplication, and because sharing in prophethood can only come from Allah, Mighty and Majestic. Ibn Qutaybah said: al-azr is the back; it is said: "I supported so-and-so in the matter," meaning I strengthened him in it and was a backing (zahr) for him in it.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and make him a partner in my affair﴾; that is, in prophethood alongside me. ﴿So that we may glorify You﴾; that is, that we may pray to You. ﴿And remember You﴾ with our tongues, praising You for the blessings You have bestowed upon us. ﴿Indeed, You have been of us ever Seeing﴾; that is, knowing, since You have singled us out with these blessings.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 20, verse 36–42:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Said, "You have been granted your request, O Moses."﴾ Ibn Qutaybah said: That is, your petition. It is (fu'l) from (sa'alta), meaning: you were given what you asked for.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And We had already conferred favor upon you another time﴾, meaning: We bestowed Our blessing upon you, ﴿another time﴾ before this time. Then He explained when it was, by His saying: ﴿When We inspired to your mother what is inspired﴾, meaning: We inspired into her heart what is inspired, which was the means of your salvation. Then He explained that by His saying: ﴿Saying, "Cast him into the chest"﴾. The "qadhf" (casting) of a thing is throwing it.

If it is asked: What is the benefit of His saying ﴿what is inspired﴾, since that is already known? Ibn al-Anbari reported two answers from him:

One of them: The meaning is: We inspired to her the thing that may be inspired to her, since not every matter is suitable to be revealed to her, because she was not a prophet; and that is because she was inspired (ulhimat).

The second: That ﴿what is inspired﴾ serves as emphasis, like His saying: ﴿So there covered them that which covered them﴾ [an-Najm: 54].

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So let it be taken up by the sea﴾. Ibn al-Anbari said: The apparent form is an imperative, but its meaning is that of a report; its interpretation: the sea will cast it up. It is permissible that the sea was commanded through an instrument which God, Exalted is He, placed in it, so that it heard and understood, just as He did with stones and trees. As for "the shore" (as-sahil), it is the bank of the sea. ﴿There will take him an enemy of Mine and an enemy of his﴾, meaning: Pharaoh. The exegetes said: His mother made a chest and placed carded cotton in it, put Moses in it, sealed the cracks of the chest with pitch, then cast him into the Nile. A great river branched from it into the house of Pharaoh. While he was sitting at the edge of the pool with his wife Asiyah, behold, there was the chest. He commanded the boys and the maids to take it. When they opened it, they saw a child of the most beautiful face among people. When Pharaoh saw him, he loved him with a intense love. This is His saying: ﴿And I bestowed upon you love from Me﴾. [Abu Ubaydah said: The meaning of "I cast upon you" is: I made for you love from Me.] Ibn Abbas said: He loved him and made him beloved to His creation, so no one met him without loving him, whether believer or disbeliever. Qatadah said: There was a charm in his eyes, so no one saw him without loving him.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And that you might be brought up under My eye﴾. Abu Ja'far recited (wa-litusna'a) with the lam and the ayn vowelless and with idgham. Qatadah said: So that you would be nourished upon My love and My will. Abu Ubaydah said: Upon what I will and love. Ibn al-Anbari said: It is from the Arabs' saying: "So-and-so was nourished under my eye," that is, under my love. Others said: So that you would be raised and nourished in view of Me. It is said: "The man raised (sana'a) his slave-girl" when he reared her, and "he raised (sana'a) his horse" when he persisted in feeding and tending to it. The meaning: "And that you might be brought up under My eye": We decreed the walking of your sister and her saying: ﴿Shall I direct you to a household that will undertake him?﴾, because this was among the means of his upbringing, according to what God, Mighty and Majestic, willed. As for his sister, Muqatil said: Her name was Maryam. Al-Farra' said: Mention is made only of the walking, (p-285) and it is not mentioned that she walked until she entered upon the family of Pharaoh and directed them to the wet-nurse, because the Arabs make do with omitting much or little of speech when the meaning is known. A similar example is His saying: ﴿I will inform you of its interpretation, so send me forth﴾ [Yusuf: 45], and He did not say "so he was sent" until he entered upon Yusuf.

The exegetes said: The reason for his sister's walking was that his mother had said to her: "Follow him." So she followed Moses along the trace of the water. When the family of Pharaoh picked him up, he would not accept the breast of any woman. His sister said to them: ﴿Shall I direct you to a household that will undertake him?﴾, that is, that will nurse him and take him to itself. It was said to her: "And who is she?" She said: "My mother." They said: "Does she have milk?" She said: "The milk of my brother Harun." Harun was three years older than Moses. So they sent her, and she came with the mother, and he accepted her breast. This is His saying: ﴿So We returned you to your mother﴾, that is, We restored you to her, ﴿that her eye might be comforted﴾ by you and by seeing you. ﴿And you killed a soul﴾, meaning the Coptic whom he struck and thereby caused his death, and its mention will come, God willing, Exalted is He. ﴿And We delivered you from distress﴾, for he had been distressed out of fear that he would be killed for it, so God saved him by his fleeing to Madyan. ﴿And We tried you with a trial﴾. In this there are three opinions:

One: We tested you with a test. Narrated by Ali ibn Abi Talhah from Ibn Abbas.

The second: We purified you with purification. Narrated by ad-Dahhak from Ibn Abbas, and Mujahid said likewise.

**The commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 20, verses 43–48:**

**His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Go, both of you, to Pharaoh﴾.** The benefit of repeating the command to go is emphasis (*tawkid*). We have already explained His saying: ﴿Indeed, he has transgressed﴾ [Ta-Ha 20:24].

**His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And speak to him with gentle speech﴾.** Abu Imran al-Jawni and Asim al-Jahdari read *layyinan* (لَيْنًا) with a sukun on the *ya*, meaning: gentle and kind.

The exegetes (*mufassirun*, those who practise *tafsir*, the science of Qur'anic exegesis) gave five opinions regarding it:

The first: "Speak to him": say, "There is no god but Allah alone, with no partner." This was narrated by Khalid ibn Ma'dan from Mu'adh, and by al-Dahhak from Ibn Abbas.

The second: it is His saying: ﴿Would you like to purify yourself? And that I guide you to your Lord so that you may fear Him﴾ [al-Nazi'at 79:18–19]. This was said by Abu Salih from Ibn Abbas, and Muqatil also said it.

The third: "Give him a kunya (teknonym)." This was narrated by Ikrimah from Ibn Abbas, and al-Suddi also said it. As for his name, we have mentioned it in *al-Baqara* [2:49]. Regarding his kunya there are four opinions: the first is Abu Murra, narrated by Ikrimah from Ibn Abbas; the second is Abu Mus'ab, mentioned by Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi; the third is Abu al-Abbas; and the fourth is Abu al-Walid. Al-Tha'labi related the last two.

The fourth opinion: "Speak to him: indeed you have a Lord, indeed you have a return, and indeed before you are a Paradise and a Fire." This was said by al-Hasan.

The fifth: the gentle speech was that Musa came to him and said: "Will you believe in what I have brought and worship the Lord of the worlds, on condition that you keep your youth and never grow old, and that you remain a king whose kingdom is not taken from you until you die; and when you die, you enter Paradise?" He was pleased with this. When Haman came, he informed him of what Musa had said, and he said: "I had thought you had sound judgment. Are you a lord who wishes to be a servant?" It is related from Yahya ibn Mu'adh that he recited this verse and said: "My God, this is Your gentleness toward one who says, 'I am a god.' So what is Your gentleness toward one who says, 'You are a god'?"

**His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Perhaps he will remember or fear﴾.** Al-Zajjaj said: "*La'alla* (لَعَلَّ, perhaps) in the language expresses hope and expectation; one says, '*La'alli asir ila khayr*' (perhaps I will arrive at good). Knowledge belongs to God, exalted is He, beyond what will occur; He knew that he would neither remember nor fear. However, the proof is established against him only through the sign and the evidence. The messengers are sent while they do not know the unseen and do not know whether it will be accepted from them, and they hope and expect that it will be accepted from them. The meaning of *la'alla* exists in their own minds, and upon this supposition the proof is established.

Ibn al-Anbari said: The position of al-Farra' on this is that it means *kay* (in order that): "that he may remember." Khalid ibn Ma'dan narrated from Mu'adh who said: "By Allah, Pharaoh did not leave this world until he had remembered or feared because of this verse; and indeed he remembered and feared when drowning overtook him."

Ka'b said: "By the One by whom Ka'b swears, it is written in the Torah: ﴿Speak to him with gentle speech; and I shall harden his heart so that he will not believe﴾."

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 20, verse 49–55:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Said, "Then who is the Lord of you two?"﴾ There is an omitted element in the speech whose meaning is known, and its implied sense is: "So they both came to him and conveyed the message." Al-Zajjaj said: "The reason he did not say 'So they both came to him' is that the speech itself contains evidence of it, since His saying 'Then who is the Lord of you two?' indicates that they came to him and spoke to him."

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Who gave everything its creation﴾ In this there are three opinions:

The first: He gave everything its form, so He created each kind of animal in other than the form of its kind. The form of the son of Adam is not like the form of cattle, and the form of the camel is not like the form of the horse. This meaning was related by al-Dahhak from Ibn ʿAbbas, and Mujahid and Saʿid ibn Jubayr also said it.

The second: He gave every male its mate. This was related by Ibn Abi Talha from Ibn ʿAbbas, and al-Suddi also said it. The meaning would then be: He gave every living thing what is suited to it.

The third: He gave everything what sets it right. This was said by Qatada.

And regarding His saying: ﴿Then guided﴾ there are three opinions:

The first: He guided it to how the male comes to the female. This was related by al-Dahhak from Ibn ʿAbbas, and Ibn Jubayr also said it.

The second: He guided it to the mate, the food, and the dwelling. This was related by Ibn Abi Talha from Ibn ʿAbbas.

The third: He guided every thing to its livelihood. Mujahid said this. ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab, Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Aʿmash, Ibn al-Sumayfaʿ, and Nusayr from al-Kisa'i read: (aʿṭā kulla shayʾin khalaqahu) with a fatha on the lam.

If it is asked: What is the basis of the argument against Pharaoh from this?

The answer: The existence of creation and guidance has been established, so there must be a Creator and a Guide.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Said, "Then what is the state of the former generations?"﴾ The scholars differed regarding what he asked about concerning the state of the former generations, in three opinions: (p-292)

The first: He asked him about their reports and accounts, and he had no knowledge of that, since the Torah had not been revealed to him until after the destruction of Pharaoh. So he said: ﴿Its knowledge is with my Lord﴾. This is the view of Muqatil. Others said: he meant, "I am a messenger, and the reports of nations are unseen knowledge, so I have no knowledge of the unseen."

The second: His purpose in asking about them was: why were idols worshipped, and why was God not worshipped, if the truth is what you describe?

The third: His purpose was: why are they not resurrected, not called to account, and not recompensed? So he said: "Their knowledge is with God," that is, the knowledge of their deeds. It was said: the pronoun in ﴿its knowledge﴾ refers to the Resurrection, since he asked him about the resurrection of the nations, and he answered him with that.

His saying: ﴿In a Book﴾ he meant: the Preserved Tablet.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿My Lord neither errs nor forgets﴾ ʿAbdullah ibn ʿAmr, ʿAsim al-Jahdari, Qatada, and Ibn Muhaysin read: (lā yuḍillu) with a damma on the ya' and a kasra on the ḍad; that is, He does not lose it. Abu al-Mutawakkil and Ibn al-Sumayfaʿ read: (lā yuḍallu) with a damma on the ya' and a fatha on the ḍad. In this verse there is an affirmation of recompense for deeds, and the meaning is: My Lord does not err nor forget what their affair was, until He recompenses them for their deeds. It was also said: he meant, "He has not placed that in a Book, because He would then err and forget."

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The One who made the earth for you a cradle﴾ Ibn Kathir, Nafiʿ, Abu ʿAmr, and Ibn ʿAmir read: (mihādan). ʿAsim, Hamzah, and al-Kisa'i read: (mahdan) without an alif. Al-mihad is the bedding, and al-mahd is the spreading. ﴿And threaded for you﴾; that is, He made roads within the earth for your sake that you may travel, ﴿and sent down from the sky water﴾, meaning: rain. (p-293) This is the last of the report about Moses. Then God, exalted is He, informed about Himself with His saying: ﴿So We brought forth thereby﴾, meaning: by the water, ﴿pairs of various plants﴾; that is, kinds differing in colors and tastes, each kind of which is a pair. It is said: "ra'a al-mashiyata yar'aha" when one drives it out to pasture. He did not see every sign of God, because they cannot be counted. ﴿But he denied﴾, that is, he attributed the signs to falsehood and said, "This is sorcery." ﴿And he refused﴾ to believe. ﴿He said, "Have you come to us to drive us out of our land﴾, meaning Egypt, ﴿with your sorcery?"﴾, that is, you want to overpower our lands with your sorcery, so that you may rule them and drive us out of them. ﴿Then we will surely bring you sorcery like it﴾, that is, we will match what you have brought of sorcery with its like. ﴿So set an appointment between us and you﴾, that is, set a fixed term and a appointed time between us and you. ﴿That neither we nor you will fail to keep﴾, that is, we will not go beyond it, ﴿at a place midway﴾. It was also said that the meaning is: set between us and you an appointment at a place where we agree to gather, and there will be no disagreement among us about attending that place.

﴿Midway (suwan)﴾: Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr and al-Kisa'i read it with a kasra on the sin (suwan). Ibn 'Amir, 'Asim, Hamzah, Khalaf and Ya'qub read it with a damma on it (suwan). Ubayy ibn Ka'b, Abu al-Mutawakkil and Ibn Abi 'Ablah read: "makanan sawa'an" (a place, equal), with the madd, the hamzah, the accusative, the tanwin, and a fatha on the sin. Ibn Mas'ud read it likewise, except that he used a kasra on the sin. Abu 'Ubaydah said: it is a noun for the middle place between the two parties, and the meaning is a place whose distance is equal for both parties, so that the distance of each party to it is like the distance of the other party.

﴿He said, "Your appointment is the day of adornment"﴾. The majority read the mim with a raf' (nominative). Al-Hasan, Mujahid, [Qatadah], Ibn Abi 'Ablah and Hubayrah from Hafs read the mim with a nasb (accusative). Regarding this day, there are four opinions:

The first: it is their festival day. This was narrated by Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas, and al-Suddi from his shaykhs, and Mujahid, Qatadah and Ibn Zayd also said so.

The second: it is the day of 'Ashura'. This was narrated by Sa'id ibn Jubayr from Ibn 'Abbas.

The third: it is the day of Nawruz, and that day coincided with Saturday, the first day of the year. This was narrated by al-Dahhak from Ibn 'Abbas.

The fourth: it is their market day. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said this.

As for the raf' of "the day", the Basrans said: the estimate is "the time of your appointment is the day of adornment," so the appointment has stood in for the time, and what would be in the nominative with the time when it is explicit has taken its place. As for its nasb (accusative), al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is "your appointment occurs on the day of adornment."

﴿And that the people be gathered﴾: the position of "an" (that) is in the nominative. The meaning is: "your appointment is the gathering of the people," ﴿in the forenoon (duha)﴾, that is, when you see the people having been gathered in the forenoon. It is permissible for "an" to be in the genitive position, in coordination with "al-zinah" (adornment), meaning: "your appointment is the day of adornment and the day of the gathering of the people in the forenoon." Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn Ya'mur and 'Asim al-Jahdari read: "wa-an tahshura" (and that you gather) with a fatha on the ta', a damma on the shin, and the nasb on "al-nas" (the people). It is also narrated from Ibn Mas'ud and al-Nakha'i: "wa-an yahshura" with a fatha on the ya' and a damma on the shin, and the nasb on "al-nas."

The exegetes said: by "the people" he meant the people of Egypt, and by "the forenoon" he meant the forenoon of that day. He only tied it to the forenoon so that the sunlight would be complete and the people would be assembled, so that the proof would be more conclusive and further from doubt.

﴿Then Pharaoh turned away﴾. On this there are two views:

One: the meaning is that he turned away from the truth that he had been commanded to follow.

The other: he withdrew to his home to prepare what he would confront Moses with. ﴿Then he gathered his scheming﴾, that is, his deception and his stratagem. ﴿Then he came﴾, that is, he attended the appointment. ﴿Moses said to them﴾, that is, to the sorcerers. We have already mentioned their number in (al-A'raf: 114).

God the Exalted said: ﴿Woe to you (waylakum)﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: it is in the accusative, as in "God has bound you to woe (waylan)," and it is permissible for it to be in the vocative, as in His saying: ﴿Woe to us! Who has raised us from our resting place?﴾ (Ya Sin: 52).

God the Exalted said: ﴿Do not invent against God a lie﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: do not associate anyone with Him.

God the Exalted said: ﴿Lest He destroy you (fa-yushihtakum)﴾. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir and Abu Bakr from 'Asim read: "fa-yasahtakum" with a fatha on the ya', from "sahata" (to uproot). Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Hafs from 'Asim read: "fa-yushihtakum" with a damma on the ya', from "ashhata." Al-Farra' said: "yusihtu" is more common, and it means uprooting. The Arabs say: "sahatahu Allah" and "ashhatahu." Al-Farazdaq said:

"The bite of time, O son of Marwan, has left of wealth only what is uprooted or stripped bare."

This is how al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj recited the verse. Abu 'Ubaydah transmitted it as "illa musahtun aw mujallafu" with a raf'.

God the Exalted said: ﴿So they disputed their affair among themselves﴾, meaning the sorcerers debated among themselves about the matter of Moses and consulted, ﴿and they concealed their private counsel (al-najwa)﴾, that is, they hid their speech from Pharaoh and his people. It was also said: from Moses and Harun. It was also said: "asarru" here means "aẓharu" (they revealed).

Regarding the words that passed among them, there are three opinions:

One: they said, "If this is a sorcerer, we will surely overcome him, and if he is from heaven, as you claim, then the matter is his." This was said by Qatadah.

The second: when they heard Moses' words, they said, "This is not the speech of a sorcerer; this is the speech of the Lord Most High." They recognised the truth, then they looked at Pharaoh and his authority, and at Moses and his staff, so they were turned upside down on their heads and said: ﴿Indeed, these two are surely sorcerers﴾. This was said by al-Dahhak and Muqatil.

The third: they said, "﴿Indeed, these two are surely sorcerers﴾ . . ." and the rest of the verses. This was said by al-Suddi.

The reciters differed regarding God the Exalted's words: ﴿Indeed, these two are surely sorcerers﴾. Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' read: "inna hadhayni," applying the operation of "inna." He said: "Indeed, I am ashamed before God to read 'inna hadhani'." Ibn Kathir read "in" light (without the shaddah), with "hadhanni" with a shaddah on the nun. 'Asim, in the narration of Hafs, read "in" light, and "hadhani" also light. Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "inna" with a shaddah, and "hadhani" with an alif and a light nun.

As for the reading of Abu 'Amr, his argument for departing from the Mushaf is what is narrated from 'Uthman and 'A'ishah, that this is a scribal error, as we have related regarding His saying: ﴿and those who establish prayer﴾ in Surat al-Nisa' (162). As for the reading of 'Asim, its meaning is: "These two are nothing but sorcerers," like His saying: ﴿And indeed we think you are among the liars﴾ (al-Shu'ara': 186), that is, we do not think you are anything but among the liars. They cited in this:

"May your mother be bereaved, if you killed a Muslim, the penalty of the deliberate killer has fallen upon him."

That is: you have killed none but a Muslim. Al-Zajjaj said: what supports this reading is what is narrated from Ubayy ibn Ka'b, that he read: "ma hadhani illa sahiran" (These two are none but sorcerers), and it is also narrated from him: "in hadhani illa sahiran" (These two are none but sorcerers). It is also narrated from al-Khalil: "in hadhani" with lightening. And there is consensus that no one was more knowledgeable in grammar than al-Khalil. As for the reading of the majority, with the shaddah on "in" and the alif in "hadhani," 'Ata' narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: it is the dialect of the Banu al-Harith ibn Ka'b. Ibn al-Anbari said: it is a dialect of the Banu al-Harith ibn Ka'b, and the dialect of Quraysh agreed with it. Al-Zajjaj said: Abu 'Ubaydah related from Abu al-Khattab, who was one of the leading transmitters, that it is a dialect of Kinanah, who make the alif of the dual in the nominative, accusative and genitive a single form, saying: "atani al-zaydan" (the two Zaydans came to me), "ra'aytu al-zaydan" (I saw the two Zaydans), and "marartu bi-al-zaydan" (I passed by the two Zaydans). They cited:

"He lowered his gaze like a lion's lowering, and if he saw a passage the lion would have bitten and struck with his teeth."

These speakers say: "I struck him between his two ears (udhunahu)." The early grammarians said: here there is a hidden hā' (pronoun), and the meaning is: "indeed, it is these two who are sorcerers." They also said: the meaning of "in" is "na'am" (yes): "Yes, these two are sorcerers." They cite:

"The women say, 'Gray hair has risen over you,' and you have grown old, so I said, 'Indeed it is.'"

Al-Zajjaj said: what I hold, and I presented it to our scholar Muhammad ibn Yazid and to Isma'il ibn Ishaq ibn Hammad ibn Zayd, and they accepted it and said it is the finest of what we have heard on this, is that "in" has taken the place of "na'am," and the meaning is: "Yes, these two have for themselves the sorcery." After this in excellence is the view of the Banu Kinanah. I consider this reading good, because it is the view of most reciters and it is the reading by which the verse is recited. I consider the reading of 'Asim and al-Khalil good, because they are two imams, and because they agreed with Ubayy ibn Ka'b in meaning. I do not permit the reading of Abu 'Amr, because it contradicts the Mushaf. Ibn al-Anbari related from al-Farra', who said: the alif of "hadhani" is the alif of "hadha," and the nun distinguishes between the singular and the dual, just as the nun of "alladhina" distinguishes between the singular and the plural.

God the Exalted said: ﴿And they would take away your ideal way of life (bi-tariqatikumu al-muthla)﴾. Abu 'Aban from 'Asim read: "wa-yudhhiba" with a damma on the ya' and a kasra on the ha'. Ibn Mas'ud, Ubayy ibn Ka'b, 'Abdullah ibn 'Amr and Abu Raja' al-'Utaridi read: "wa-yadhhaba bi-al-tariqah" with an alif and lam, with the omission of the kaf and the mim.

On "al-tariqah" there are two views:

One: "with your upright religion," narrated by al-Dahhak from Ibn 'Abbas. Abu 'Ubaydah said: with your sunnah, your religion, and what you are upon. It is said: "so-and-so has a good tariqah."

The other: "with your best people." This was narrated by Ibn Abi Talhah from Ibn 'Abbas. Mujahid said: with the people of intellect, nobility and age. Al-Sha'bi said: they turn the faces of the people toward themselves. Al-Farra' said: "al-tariqah" means the noble men. The Arabs say of a noble people: "these are the tariqah of their people," and "tara'iq of their people."

As for "al-muthla," Abu 'Ubaydah said: it is the feminine form of "al-amthal" (the best). They say for females: "take the muthla of them both," and for males: "take the amthal." Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning of "al-muthla" and "al-amthal" is: the one of merit by which he deserves to be said, "This is the best of his people." He said: what I think is that there is an omitted element in the speech, and the meaning is: "they would take away with the people of your best tariqah," and the Arabs' saying "this is the tariqah of his people" means "the owner of their tariqah."

God the Exalted said: ﴿So settle your scheme (fa-ajmi'u kaydakum)﴾. The majority read: "fa-ajmi'u" with the cutting of the alif, from "ajma'tu" (I resolved). The meaning: your resolve should be settled upon, do not differ lest your affair fall into disorder. Al-Farra' said: al-ijma' (resolving) means firmness and determination upon a thing. You say: "ajma'tu 'ala al-khuruj" (I resolved upon going out), and "ajma'tu al-khuruja" (I resolved the going out), meaning "azmatu" (I determined). The poet said:

"Would that I knew, though wishes do not benefit, whether I will go forth one day while my matter is resolved?"

He means: "I have determined and resolved upon it." Abu 'Amr read: "fa-ajma'u" with a fatha on the mim, from "jama'tu" (I gathered), meaning: do not leave any of your scheming without bringing it. As for "kaydahum", the intended meaning is their sorcery and their deception.

God the Exalted said: ﴿Then come in ranks (saffan)﴾, that is, lined up, gathered together, so that your affairs are more orderly and your awe is greater. Abu 'Ubaydah said: "saffan" means rows. Ibn Qutaybah said: "saffan" means together, as a group. Al-Hasan said: they were twenty-five rows, each thousand sorcerers a row.

God the Exalted said: ﴿And indeed he has succeeded today, who has prevailed (istala)﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: he who overcomes has succeeded.

The Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on Surah 20, verses 56–64:

He did not see every sign of God, because they cannot be counted. ﴿But he denied﴾, that is, he attributed the signs to falsehood and said, "This is sorcery." ﴿And he refused﴾ to believe. ﴿He said, "Have you come to us to drive us out of our land﴾, meaning Egypt, ﴿with your sorcery?"﴾, that is, you want to overpower our lands with your sorcery, so that you may rule them and drive us out of them. ﴿Then we will surely bring you sorcery like it﴾, that is, we will match what you have brought of sorcery with its like. ﴿So set an appointment between us and you﴾, that is, set a fixed term and a appointed time between us and you. ﴿That neither we nor you will fail to keep﴾, that is, we will not go beyond it, ﴿at a place midway﴾. It was also said that the meaning is: set between us and you an appointment at a place where we agree to gather, and there will be no disagreement among us about attending that place.

﴿Midway (suwan)﴾: Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr and al-Kisa'i read it with a kasra on the sin (suwan). Ibn 'Amir, 'Asim, Hamzah, Khalaf and Ya'qub read it with a damma on it (suwan). Ubayy ibn Ka'b, Abu al-Mutawakkil and Ibn Abi 'Ablah read: "makanan sawa'an" (a place, equal), with the madd, the hamzah, the accusative, the tanwin, and a fatha on the sin. Ibn Mas'ud read it likewise, except that he used a kasra on the sin. Abu 'Ubaydah said: it is a noun for the middle place between the two parties, and the meaning is a place whose distance is equal for both parties, so that the distance of each party to it is like the distance of the other party.

The first: it is their festival day. This was narrated by Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas, and al-Suddi from his shaykhs, and Mujahid, Qatadah and Ibn Zayd also said so.

The second: it is the day of 'Ashura'. This was narrated by Sa'id ibn Jubayr from Ibn 'Abbas.

The third: it is the day of Nawruz, and that day coincided with Saturday, the first day of the year. This was narrated by al-Dahhak from Ibn 'Abbas.

The fourth: it is their market day. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said this.

As for the raf' of "the day", the Basrans said: the estimate is "the time of your appointment is the day of adornment," so the appointment has stood in for the time, and what would be in the nominative with the time when it is explicit has taken its place. As for its nasb (accusative), al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is "your appointment occurs on the day of adornment."

The meaning is: "your appointment is the gathering of the people," ﴿in the forenoon (duha)﴾, that is, when you see the people having been gathered in the forenoon. The exegetes said: by "the people" he meant the people of Egypt, and by "the forenoon" he meant the forenoon of that day. He only tied it to the forenoon so that the sunlight would be complete and the people would be assembled, so that the proof would be more conclusive and further from doubt.

﴿Then Pharaoh turned away﴾. On this there are two views:

One: the meaning is that he turned away from the truth that he had been commanded to follow.

The other: he withdrew to his home to prepare what he would confront Moses with. ﴿Then he gathered his scheming﴾, that is, his deception and his stratagem. ﴿Then he came﴾, that is, he attended the appointment. ﴿Moses said to them﴾, that is, to the sorcerers. We have already mentioned their number in (al-A'raf: 114).

God the Exalted said: ﴿Woe to you (waylakum)﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: it is in the accusative, as in "God has bound you to woe (waylan)," and it is permissible for it to be in the vocative, as in His saying: ﴿Woe to us! Who has raised us from our resting place?﴾ (Ya Sin: 52).

God the Exalted said: ﴿Do not invent against God a lie﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: do not associate anyone with Him.

God the Exalted said: ﴿Lest He destroy you (fa-yushihtakum)﴾. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir and Abu Bakr from 'Asim read: "fa-yasahtakum" with a fatha on the ya', from "sahata" (to uproot). "The bite of time, O son of Marwan, has left of wealth only what is uprooted or stripped bare."

This is how al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj recited the verse. Abu 'Ubaydah transmitted it as "illa musahtun aw mujallafu" with a raf'.

The second: it is the day of 'Ashura'. This was narrated by Sa'id ibn Jubayr from Ibn 'Abbas.

The third: it is the day of Nawruz, and that day coincided with Saturday, the first day of the year. This was narrated by al-Dahhak from Ibn 'Abbas.

One: the meaning is that he turned away from the truth that he had been commanded to follow.
