Al-Zajjaj said: Abu 'Ubaydah related from Abu al-Khattab, who was one of the leading transmitters, that it is a dialect of Kinanah, who make the alif of the dual in the nominative, accusative and genitive a single form, saying: "atani al-zaydan" (the two Zaydans came to me), "ra'aytu al-zaydan" (I saw the two Zaydans), and "marartu bi-al-zaydan" (I passed by the two Zaydans). They cited:

"He lowered his gaze like a lion's lowering, and if he saw a passage the lion would have bitten and struck with his teeth."

These speakers say: "I struck him between his two ears (udhunahu)." The early grammarians said: here there is a hidden hā' (pronoun), and the meaning is: "indeed, it is these two who are sorcerers." They also said: the meaning of "in" is "na'am" (yes): "Yes, these two are sorcerers." They cite:

"The women say, 'Gray hair has risen over you,' and you have grown old, so I said, 'Indeed it is.'"

Al-Zajjaj said: what I hold, and I presented it to our scholar Muhammad ibn Yazid and to Isma'il ibn Ishaq ibn Hammad ibn Zayd, and they accepted it and said it is the finest of what we have heard on this, is that "in" has taken the place of "na'am," and the meaning is: "Yes, these two have for themselves the sorcery." After this in excellence is the view of the Banu Kinanah. I consider this reading good, because it is the view of most reciters and it is the reading by which the verse is recited. I consider the reading of 'Asim and al-Khalil good, because they are two imams, and because they agreed with Ubayy ibn Ka'b in meaning. I do not permit the reading of Abu 'Amr, because it contradicts the Mushaf. Ibn al-Anbari related from al-Farra', who said: the alif of "hadhani" is the alif of "hadha," and the nun distinguishes between the singular and the dual, just as the nun of "alladhina" distinguishes between the singular and the plural.

God the Exalted said: ﴿And they would take away your ideal way of life (bi-tariqatikumu al-muthla)﴾. Abu 'Aban from 'Asim read: "wa-yudhhiba" with a damma on the ya' and a kasra on the ha'. Ibn Mas'ud, Ubayy ibn Ka'b, 'Abdullah ibn 'Amr and Abu Raja' al-'Utaridi read: "wa-yadhhaba bi-al-tariqah" with an alif and lam, with the omission of the kaf and the mim.

On "al-tariqah" there are two views:

One: "with your upright religion," narrated by al-Dahhak from Ibn 'Abbas. Abu 'Ubaydah said: with your sunnah, your religion, and what you are upon. It is said: "so-and-so has a good tariqah."

The other: "with your best people." This was narrated by Ibn Abi Talhah from Ibn 'Abbas. Mujahid said: with the people of intellect, nobility and age. Al-Sha'bi said: they turn the faces of the people toward themselves. Al-Farra' said: "al-tariqah" means the noble men. The Arabs say of a noble people: "these are the tariqah of their people," and "tara'iq of their people."

As for "al-muthla," Abu 'Ubaydah said: it is the feminine form of "al-amthal" (the best). They say for females: "take the muthla of them both," and for males: "take the amthal." Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning of "al-muthla" and "al-amthal" is: the one of merit by which he deserves to be said, "This is the best of his people." He said: what I think is that there is an omitted element in the speech, and the meaning is: "they would take away with the people of your best tariqah," and the Arabs' saying "this is the tariqah of his people" means "the owner of their tariqah."

God the Exalted said: ﴿So settle your scheme (fa-ajmi'u kaydakum)﴾. The majority read: "fa-ajmi'u" with the cutting of the alif, from "ajma'tu" (I resolved). The meaning: your resolve should be settled upon, do not differ lest your affair fall into disorder. Al-Farra' said: al-ijma' (resolving) means firmness and determination upon a thing. You say: "ajma'tu 'ala al-khuruj" (I resolved upon going out), and "ajma'tu al-khuruja" (I resolved the going out), meaning "azmatu" (I determined). The poet said:

"Would that I knew, though wishes do not benefit, whether I will go forth one day while my matter is resolved?"

He means: "I have determined and resolved upon it." Abu 'Amr read: "fa-ajma'u" with a fatha on the mim, from "jama'tu" (I gathered), meaning: do not leave any of your scheming without bringing it. As for "kaydahum", the intended meaning is their sorcery and their deception.

God the Exalted said: ﴿Then come in ranks (saffan)﴾, that is, lined up, gathered together, so that your affairs are more orderly and your awe is greater. Abu 'Ubaydah said: "saffan" means rows. Ibn Qutaybah said: "saffan" means together, as a group. Al-Hasan said: they were twenty-five rows, each thousand sorcerers a row.

God the Exalted said: ﴿And indeed he has succeeded today, who has prevailed (istala)﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: he who overcomes has succeeded.

The Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on Surah 20, verses 56–64:

God the Exalted said: ﴿And We showed him all Our signs﴾, meaning Pharaoh, ﴿all Our signs﴾, meaning the nine signs. He did not see every sign of God, because they cannot be counted. ﴿But he denied﴾, that is, he attributed the signs to falsehood and said, "This is sorcery." ﴿And he refused﴾ to believe. ﴿He said, "Have you come to us to drive us out of our land﴾, meaning Egypt, ﴿with your sorcery?"﴾, that is, you want to overpower our lands with your sorcery, so that you may rule them and drive us out of them. ﴿Then we will surely bring you sorcery like it﴾, that is, we will match what you have brought of sorcery with its like. ﴿So set an appointment between us and you﴾, that is, set a fixed term and a appointed time between us and you. ﴿That neither we nor you will fail to keep﴾, that is, we will not go beyond it, ﴿at a place midway﴾. It was also said that the meaning is: set between us and you an appointment at a place where we agree to gather, and there will be no disagreement among us about attending that place.

﴿Midway (suwan)﴾: Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr and al-Kisa'i read it with a kasra on the sin (suwan). Ibn 'Amir, 'Asim, Hamzah, Khalaf and Ya'qub read it with a damma on it (suwan). Ubayy ibn Ka'b, Abu al-Mutawakkil and Ibn Abi 'Ablah read: "makanan sawa'an" (a place, equal), with the madd, the hamzah, the accusative, the tanwin, and a fatha on the sin. Ibn Mas'ud read it likewise, except that he used a kasra on the sin. Abu 'Ubaydah said: it is a noun for the middle place between the two parties, and the meaning is a place whose distance is equal for both parties, so that the distance of each party to it is like the distance of the other party.

﴿He said, "Your appointment is the day of adornment"﴾. The majority read the mim with a raf' (nominative). Al-Hasan, Mujahid, [Qatadah], Ibn Abi 'Ablah and Hubayrah from Hafs read the mim with a nasb (accusative). Regarding this day, there are four opinions:

The first: it is their festival day. This was narrated by Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas, and al-Suddi from his shaykhs, and Mujahid, Qatadah and Ibn Zayd also said so.

The second: it is the day of 'Ashura'. This was narrated by Sa'id ibn Jubayr from Ibn 'Abbas.

The third: it is the day of Nawruz, and that day coincided with Saturday, the first day of the year. This was narrated by al-Dahhak from Ibn 'Abbas.

The fourth: it is their market day. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said this.

As for the raf' of "the day", the Basrans said: the estimate is "the time of your appointment is the day of adornment," so the appointment has stood in for the time, and what would be in the nominative with the time when it is explicit has taken its place. As for its nasb (accusative), al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is "your appointment occurs on the day of adornment."

﴿And that the people be gathered﴾: the position of "an" (that) is in the nominative. The meaning is: "your appointment is the gathering of the people," ﴿in the forenoon (duha)﴾, that is, when you see the people having been gathered in the forenoon. It is permissible for "an" to be in the genitive position, in coordination with "al-zinah" (adornment), meaning: "your appointment is the day of adornment and the day of the gathering of the people in the forenoon." Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn Ya'mur and 'Asim al-Jahdari read: "wa-an tahshura" (and that you gather) with a fatha on the ta', a damma on the shin, and the nasb on "al-nas" (the people). It is also narrated from Ibn Mas'ud and al-Nakha'i: "wa-an yahshura" with a fatha on the ya' and a damma on the shin, and the nasb on "al-nas."

The exegetes said: by "the people" he meant the people of Egypt, and by "the forenoon" he meant the forenoon of that day. He only tied it to the forenoon so that the sunlight would be complete and the people would be assembled, so that the proof would be more conclusive and further from doubt.

﴿Then Pharaoh turned away﴾. On this there are two views:

One: the meaning is that he turned away from the truth that he had been commanded to follow.

The other: he withdrew to his home to prepare what he would confront Moses with. ﴿Then he gathered his scheming﴾, that is, his deception and his stratagem. ﴿Then he came﴾, that is, he attended the appointment. ﴿Moses said to them﴾, that is, to the sorcerers. We have already mentioned their number in (al-A'raf: 114).

God the Exalted said: ﴿Woe to you (waylakum)﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: it is in the accusative, as in "God has bound you to woe (waylan)," and it is permissible for it to be in the vocative, as in His saying: ﴿Woe to us! Who has raised us from our resting place?﴾ (Ya Sin: 52).

God the Exalted said: ﴿Do not invent against God a lie﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: do not associate anyone with Him.

God the Exalted said: ﴿Lest He destroy you (fa-yushihtakum)﴾. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir and Abu Bakr from 'Asim read: "fa-yasahtakum" with a fatha on the ya', from "sahata" (to uproot). Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Hafs from 'Asim read: "fa-yushihtakum" with a damma on the ya', from "ashhata." Al-Farra' said: "yusihtu" is more common, and it means uprooting. The Arabs say: "sahatahu Allah" and "ashhatahu." Al-Farazdaq said:

"The bite of time, O son of Marwan, has left of wealth only what is uprooted or stripped bare."

This is how al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj recited the verse. Abu 'Ubaydah transmitted it as "illa musahtun aw mujallafu" with a raf'.

God the Exalted said: ﴿So they disputed their affair among themselves﴾, meaning the sorcerers debated among themselves about the matter of Moses and consulted, ﴿and they concealed their private counsel (al-najwa)﴾, that is, they hid their speech from Pharaoh and his people. It was also said: from Moses and Harun. It was also said: "asarru" here means "aẓharu" (they revealed).

Regarding the words that passed among them, there are three opinions:

One: they said, "If this is a sorcerer, we will surely overcome him, and if he is from heaven, as you claim, then the matter is his." This was said by Qatadah.

The second: when they heard Moses' words, they said, "This is not the speech of a sorcerer; this is the speech of the Lord Most High." They recognised the truth, then they looked at Pharaoh and his authority, and at Moses and his staff, so they were turned upside down on their heads and said: ﴿Indeed, these two are surely sorcerers﴾. This was said by al-Dahhak and Muqatil.

The third: they said, "﴿Indeed, these two are surely sorcerers﴾ . . ." and the rest of the verses. This was said by al-Suddi.

The reciters differed regarding God the Exalted's words: ﴿Indeed, these two are surely sorcerers﴾. Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' read: "inna hadhayni," applying the operation of "inna." He said: "Indeed, I am ashamed before God to read 'inna hadhani'." Ibn Kathir read "in" light (without the shaddah), with "hadhanni" with a shaddah on the nun. 'Asim, in the narration of Hafs, read "in" light, and "hadhani" also light. Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "inna" with a shaddah, and "hadhani" with an alif and a light nun.

As for the reading of Abu 'Amr, his argument for departing from the Mushaf is what is narrated from 'Uthman and 'A'ishah, that this is a scribal error, as we have related regarding His saying: ﴿and those who establish prayer﴾ in Surat al-Nisa' (162). As for the reading of 'Asim, its meaning is: "These two are nothing but sorcerers," like His saying: ﴿And indeed we think you are among the liars﴾ (al-Shu'ara': 186), that is, we do not think you are anything but among the liars. They cited in this:

"May your mother be bereaved, if you killed a Muslim, the penalty of the deliberate killer has fallen upon him."

That is: you have killed none but a Muslim. Al-Zajjaj said: what supports this reading is what is narrated from Ubayy ibn Ka'b, that he read: "ma hadhani illa sahiran" (These two are none but sorcerers), and it is also narrated from him: "in hadhani illa sahiran" (These two are none but sorcerers). It is also narrated from al-Khalil: "in hadhani" with lightening. And there is consensus that no one was more knowledgeable in grammar than al-Khalil. On "al-tariqah" there are two views:

One: "with your upright religion," narrated by al-Dahhak from Ibn 'Abbas. Abu 'Ubaydah said: with your sunnah, your religion, and what you are upon. It is said: "so-and-so has a good tariqah."

The other: "with your best people." This was narrated by Ibn Abi Talhah from Ibn 'Abbas. Mujahid said: with the people of intellect, nobility and age. The meaning: your resolve should be settled upon, do not differ lest your affair fall into disorder. Al-Farra' said: al-ijma' (resolving) means firmness and determination upon a thing. You say: "ajma'tu 'ala al-khuruj" (I resolved upon going out), and "ajma'tu al-khuruja" (I resolved the going out), meaning "azmatu" (I determined). The poet said:

"Would that I knew, though wishes do not benefit, whether I will go forth one day while my matter is resolved?"

Ibn Qutaybah said: "saffan" means together, as a group. Al-Hasan said: they were twenty-five rows, each thousand sorcerers a row.

God the Exalted said: ﴿And indeed he has succeeded today, who has prevailed (istala)﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: he who overcomes has succeeded.

"Then cast" — Ibn al-Anbari said: "Bal" (rather) has entered for a meaning that was denied in the first verse, because the first verse, when considered, contains [the alternatives]: either you cast, or you do not cast.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And their ropes⁠﴾ (wa-'isiyyuhum). Al-Hasan, Abu Raja' al-'Utaridi, Abu 'Imran al-Jawni, and Abu al-Jawza' read it as (wa-'usiyyuhum), with a damma on the 'ayn.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿It was imagined to him⁠﴾ (yukhayyalu ilayhi). Abu Razin al-'Uqayli, Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami, al-Hasan, Qatada, al-Zuhri, and Ibn Abi 'Abla read it as (tukhayyalu), with a ta'. ﴿To him⁠﴾, i.e., to Musa. It is said: khuyyila ilayhi, meaning it was made to appear to him. Some people have used this verse as evidence that magic is nothing real, and they said: "It was only imagined to Musa." The reply: We do not deny that what Musa saw was an illusion and not a reality, for it is permissible that they had placed mercury in the channels of the snakes until they moved, and those were not actual snakes.

As for magic, it does have an effect, and it comes in various kinds. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was bewitched until its effect appeared on him, and he cursed the 'adhiha, which is the female magician.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿So Musa sensed within himself a fear⁠﴾. Ibn Qutayba said: he concealed within himself fear. Al-Zajjaj said: its original form was (khuwifa), but the waw was changed to a ya' because of the kasra before it.

Regarding khiyfa (fear) there are two opinions:

One: that it was the natural fear of the human disposition.

The second: that when he saw their magic was of the same kind as what he had shown them in the staff, he feared that the matter would be confused for the people and they would not believe. So it was said to him: ﴿Do not fear; indeed, you are the superior⁠﴾ over them by victory and triumph. This second view is more sound than the first.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And throw what is in your right hand⁠﴾, meaning the staff. ﴿It will swallow⁠﴾ (talqaf). Ibn 'Amir read (talaqqafu ma) with a damma on the fa' and a shadda on the qaf. Hafs related from 'Asim (talqaf) with a light pronunciation. Ibn Kathir used to pronounce the ta' of (talqaf) with a shadda, meaning (tatalaqqaf). Ibn Mas'ud, Ubayy ibn Ka'b, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, and Abu Raja' read (talqam) with a mim. We have explained it in (al-A'raf: 117).

﴿What they have made is only the trick of a magician⁠﴾. Hamza, al-Kisa'i, and Khalaf read (kaydu al-sihr). The rest read (kaydu sahir) with an alif, and the meaning is: what they made is the trick of a magician, i.e., the work of a magician. Ibn Mas'ud and Abu 'Imran al-Jawni read (innama sana'u kayda) with a fatha on the dal. ﴿And the magician does not succeed⁠﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: he does not prosper wherever he is. It was also said: he does not win. Jundab ibn 'Abd Allah al-Bajali narrated that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "If you capture a magician, kill him," then he recited: ﴿And the magician does not succeed wherever he comes⁠﴾, and said: he is not safe wherever he is found.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿He said, "Have you believed in him?"⁠﴾ Ibn Kathir, Hafs from 'Asim, and Warsh from Nafi' read (amantum lahu) in the form of a statement. Nafi', Abu 'Amr, and Ibn 'Amir read (amantum lahu) with a long hamza. Hamza, al-Kisa'i, and Abu Bakr from 'Asim read (a'amantum lahu) with two hamzas, the second being lengthened. (p-307)

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, he is your chief⁠﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: he means your teacher. Al-Kisa'i said: a boy in the Hijaz, when he comes from his teacher, says: "I came from my kabir (chief)."

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And I will surely crucify you on the trunks of palm trees⁠﴾. "Fi" here means "'ala" (on), and similar to it is: ﴿Or do they have a ladder by which they listen therein?⁠﴾ [al-Tur: 38]. ﴿And you will surely know⁠﴾, O magicians, ﴿which of us is more severe in punishment⁠﴾ upon you, ﴿and more enduring⁠﴾, i.e., more lasting: is it I regarding your faith, or the Lord of Musa regarding your abandonment of belief in Him? ﴿They said, "We will not prefer you⁠﴾, i.e., we will not choose you, ﴿over what has come to us of clear evidences⁠﴾, meaning the hand and the staff.

If it is asked: Why did they attribute the signs to themselves by saying ﴿came to us⁠﴾, when they came generally for them and for others?

The answer: Since they were more knowledgeable than others in the doors of magic and the methods of trickery, and they knew that what Musa had brought was not magic, it was clearer and more manifest with respect to others, and they were more specifically aware of it because of their knowledge.

Regarding His saying ﴿and He who originated us⁠﴾ there are two views, mentioned by al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj:

One: the meaning is: we will not prefer you over what has come to us of clear evidences and over He who originated us.

The second: that it is an oath, its implied sense being: "By the right of He who originated us."

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿So decide what you are going to decide⁠﴾, i.e., do what you are going to do. The root of qada' (decision) is work done with firmness. ﴿You can only decide upon this worldly life⁠﴾. Al-Farra' said: ﴿innama⁠﴾ is a single particle; therefore ﴿al-hayat al-dunya⁠﴾ is in the accusative. Had a reader read (al-hayatu) in the nominative, it would be permissible, taking (ma) in the sense of (alladhi), as in your saying: "Indeed, what decides is this worldly life." Ibn Abi 'Abla and Abu al-Mutawakkil read (innama tuqda) with a damma on the ta', in the passive, and (al-hayatu) with a damma on the ta'. The exegetes said: the meaning is that your authority and your sovereignty are only in this world, not in the Hereafter. (p-308)

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿That He may forgive us our sins⁠﴾, meaning shirk, ﴿and what you compelled us to⁠﴾, i.e., and what you compelled us to; that is, and He may forgive us for your compelling us to magic.

If it is asked: How did they say "you compelled us," when they had said "Indeed, will there be a reward for us?" and this indicates that they performed magic without being compelled? There are four answers regarding this:

One: that Pharaoh used to compel people to learn magic, as said by Ibn 'Abbas. Ibn al-Anbari said: he would demand of some people in his kingdom that they teach their children magic while they were unwilling, owing to his passion for magic and the fear of Musa that had taken root in his heart. So compulsion to magic is compulsion to learn it at the outset.

The second: that when the magicians witnessed Musa after their saying "Will there be a reward for us?", and saw his remembrance of Allah the Exalted and his following the path of the righteous, they feared meeting him with magic and dreaded that he would prevail over them and discover the weakness of their craft, so their livelihood would be ruined. Pharaoh was satisfied from them only with opposing Musa, and this was the compulsion to magic.

The third: that they feared being defeated in that gathering, which would harm their craft before the kings and in the markets, and Pharaoh compelled them to perform magic.

Had a reader read (al-hayatu) in the nominative, it would be permissible, taking (ma) in the sense of (alladhi), as in your saying: "Indeed, what decides is this worldly life." Ibn Abi 'Abla and Abu al-Mutawakkil read (innama tuqda) with a damma on the ta', in the passive, and (al-hayatu) with a damma on the ta'. The exegetes said: the meaning is that your authority and your sovereignty are only in this world, not in the Hereafter. (p-308)

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿That He may forgive us our sins⁠﴾, meaning shirk, ﴿and what you compelled us to⁠﴾, i.e., and what you compelled us to; that is, and He may forgive us for your compelling us to magic.

If it is asked: How did they say "you compelled us," when they had said "Indeed, will there be a reward for us?" and this indicates that they performed magic without being compelled? There are four answers regarding this:

One: that Pharaoh used to compel people to learn magic, as said by Ibn 'Abbas. Ibn al-Anbari said: he would demand of some people in his kingdom that they teach their children magic while they were unwilling, owing to his passion for magic and the fear of Musa that had taken root in his heart. So compulsion to magic is compulsion to learn it at the outset.

The second: that when the magicians witnessed Musa after their saying "Will there be a reward for us?", and saw his remembrance of Allah the Exalted and his following the path of the righteous, they feared meeting him with magic and dreaded that he would prevail over them and discover the weakness of their craft, so their livelihood would be ruined. Pharaoh was satisfied from them only with opposing Musa, and this was the compulsion to magic.

The third: that they feared being defeated in that gathering, which would harm their craft before the kings and in the markets, and Pharaoh compelled them to perform magic.

The fourth: that Pharaoh compelled them to leave their homelands, and the cause of that was magic. Ibn al-Anbari mentioned these views.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And Allah is better⁠﴾, i.e., better than you in reward if obeyed, ﴿and more enduring⁠﴾ in punishment if disobeyed. This is the answer to His saying: ﴿And you will surely know which of us is more severe in punishment and more enduring.⁠﴾ This is the end of the report concerning the magicians.

"Then cast" — Ibn al-Anbari said: "Bal" (rather) has entered for a meaning that was denied in the first verse, because the first verse, when considered, contains [the alternatives]: either you cast, or you do not cast.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And their ropes⁠﴾ (wa-'isiyyuhum). Al-Hasan, Abu Raja' al-'Utaridi, Abu 'Imran al-Jawni, and Abu al-Jawza' read it as (wa-'usiyyuhum), with a damma on the 'ayn.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿It was imagined to him⁠﴾ (yukhayyalu ilayhi). Abu Razin al-'Uqayli, Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami, al-Hasan, Qatada, al-Zuhri, and Ibn Abi 'Abla read it as (tukhayyalu), with a ta'. ﴿To him⁠﴾, i.e., to Musa. It is said: khuyyila ilayhi, meaning it was made to appear to him. Some people have used this verse as evidence that magic is nothing real, and they said: "It was only imagined to Musa." The reply: We do not deny that what Musa saw was an illusion and not a reality, for it is permissible that they had placed mercury in the channels of the snakes until they moved, and those were not actual snakes.

As for magic, it does have an effect, and it comes in various kinds. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was bewitched until its effect appeared on him, and he cursed the 'adhiha, which is the female magician.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿So Musa sensed within himself a fear⁠﴾. Ibn Qutayba said: he concealed within himself fear. Al-Zajjaj said: its original form was (khuwifa), but the waw was changed to a ya' because of the kasra before it.

Regarding khiyfa (fear) there are two opinions:

One: that it was the natural fear of the human disposition.

The second: that when he saw their magic was of the same kind as what he had shown them in the staff, he feared that the matter would be confused for the people and they would not believe. So it was said to him: ﴿Do not fear; indeed, you are the superior⁠﴾ over them by victory and triumph. This second view is more sound than the first.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And throw what is in your right hand⁠﴾, meaning the staff. ﴿It will swallow⁠﴾ (talqaf). Ibn 'Amir read (talaqqafu ma) with a damma on the fa' and a shadda on the qaf. Hafs related from 'Asim (talqaf) with a light pronunciation. Ibn Kathir used to pronounce the ta' of (talqaf) with a shadda, meaning (tatalaqqaf). Ibn Mas'ud, Ubayy ibn Ka'b, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, and Abu Raja' read (talqam) with a mim. We have explained it in (al-A'raf: 117).

﴿What they have made is only the trick of a magician⁠﴾. Hamza, al-Kisa'i, and Khalaf read (kaydu al-sihr). The rest read (kaydu sahir) with an alif, and the meaning is: what they made is the trick of a magician, i.e., the work of a magician. Ibn Mas'ud and Abu 'Imran al-Jawni read (innama sana'u kayda) with a fatha on the dal. ﴿And the magician does not succeed⁠﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: he does not prosper wherever he is. It was also said: he does not win. Jundab ibn 'Abd Allah al-Bajali narrated that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "If you capture a magician, kill him," then he recited: ﴿And the magician does not succeed wherever he comes⁠﴾, and said: he is not safe wherever he is found.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿He said, "Have you believed in him?"⁠﴾ Ibn Kathir, Hafs from 'Asim, and Warsh from Nafi' read (amantum lahu) in the form of a statement. Nafi', Abu 'Amr, and Ibn 'Amir read (amantum lahu) with a long hamza. Hamza, al-Kisa'i, and Abu Bakr from 'Asim read (a'amantum lahu) with two hamzas, the second being lengthened. (p-307)

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, he is your chief⁠﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: he means your teacher. Al-Kisa'i said: a boy in the Hijaz, when he comes from his teacher, says: "I came from my kabir (chief)."

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And I will surely crucify you on the trunks of palm trees⁠﴾. "Fi" here means "'ala" (on), and similar to it is: ﴿Or do they have a ladder by which they listen therein?⁠﴾ [al-Tur: 38]. ﴿And you will surely know⁠﴾, O magicians, ﴿which of us is more severe in punishment⁠﴾ upon you, ﴿and more enduring⁠﴾, i.e., more lasting: is it I regarding your faith, or the Lord of Musa regarding your abandonment of belief in Him? ﴿They said, "We will not prefer you⁠﴾, i.e., we will not choose you, ﴿over what has come to us of clear evidences⁠﴾, meaning the hand and the staff.

If it is asked: Why did they attribute the signs to themselves by saying ﴿came to us⁠﴾, when they came generally for them and for others?

The answer: Since they were more knowledgeable than others in the doors of magic and the methods of trickery, and they knew that what Musa had brought was not magic, it was clearer and more manifest with respect to others, and they were more specifically aware of it because of their knowledge.

One: the meaning is: we will not prefer you over what has come to us of clear evidences and over He who originated us.

The second: that it is an oath, its implied sense being: "By the right of He who originated us."

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 20, verses 74–76:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, whoever comes to his Lord as a criminal﴾ means: an associator (mushrik), ﴿for him is Hell; he will neither die therein⁠﻿ and [thus] find rest, nor live⁠﻿ a life that benefits him.﴾

[Ibn al-Anbari recited, regarding this same meaning, the verse:

Is there anyone for a soul that does not die, so that its misery ends, nor lives a life that has any sweetness to it?]

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿But whoever comes to Him as a believer, having done righteous deeds﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: [it means] he has performed the obligatory duties (al-fara'id). ﴿For those are the high ranks⁠﻿﴾ means: the ranks of Paradise, some of which are higher than others. Al-'Ula is the plural of al-'Ulya, which is the feminine of al-A'la (the highest). Ibn al-Anbari said: He said ﴿for those﴾ (fa-ulaika) because "man" (man) is used in the singular form while carrying the meaning of the plural. When its wording is dominant, the pronoun referring back to it is put in the singular; when its meaning is made explicit, the pronoun referring to it is put in the plural.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And that﴾ means: the reward, ﴿is the recompense of one who purifies himself﴾; i.e., cleansed himself from disbelief and sins.

﴿That bring out My servants by night﴾; that is, travel with them by night from the land of Egypt. ﴿Strike for them a dry path﴾; that is, make for them a path ﴿through the sea, dry﴾. Abu al-Mutawakkil, al-Hasan and al-Nakha'i read *yabsan* (يَبْسًا) with the *ba'* sukun. Al-Sha'bi, Abu Raja' and Ibn al-Sumayfa' read *yabisan* (يابِسًا) with an alif. Abu 'Ubayda said: *al-yabas* (اليَبَسُ) has a moving final letter and means the same as *al-yabis* (اليابِس, "dry"). It is said: *shatun yabas* (شاةٌ يَبَسٌ), that is, a dry ewe that has no milk. Ibn Qutayba said: *yabas* and *yabs* are both used for "dry."

﴿You will not fear﴾: most readers use the alif (*la takhafu*, لا تَخافُ). Aban and Hamza, on the authority of 'Asim, read *la takhaf* (لا تَخَفْ). Al-Zajjaj said: whoever reads *la takhafu* means "you do not fear," and whoever reads *la takhaf* makes it a prohibition against fear. Al-Farra' said: Hamza read *la takhaf* in the jussive, and *wa la takhsha* (ولا تَخْشى) in the nominative, as a new sentence (*isti'naf*), like the verse ﴿They will turn their backs to you, then they will not be helped﴾ (Al 'Imran: 111), where the sentence is begun with *thumma* ("then"). This is similar to it. Had Hamza intended the jussive for *wa la takhsha* as well, even though the *ya'* is present, it would have been correct. Ibn Qutayba said: the meaning of ﴿*darakan*﴾ is "overtaking" (*lihaq*).

The commentators said: the companions of Musa said, "This is Pharaoh, who has overtaken us, and this sea is before us." So God revealed to Musa: ﴿Do not fear being overtaken﴾, that is, by Pharaoh, ﴿nor fear﴾ drowning in the sea.

﴿Then Pharaoh pursued them﴾: Ibn Qutayba said: he overtook them. Harun reported from Abu 'Amr: *fattaba'ahum* (فاتَّبَعَهم) with the doubled *ta'*. Al-Zajjaj said: *taba'a al-rajulu al-shay'a* and *atba'ahu* have the same meaning. Whoever reads with the doubling has evidence that he followed them with his troops. Whoever reads *fa-atba'ahum* (فَأتْبَعَهم) means he caused his troops to overtake them. It is possible that he was with them according to this reading, and it is possible that he was not, though he was indeed with them. ﴿Then the sea covered them with what covered them﴾; that is, the water of the sea covered them, which drowned them. Ibn al-Anbari said: by ﴿what covered them﴾ he means a part of what covered them, since not all of its water covered them. Ibn Mas'ud, 'Ikrima, Abu Raja' and al-A'mash read *fa-ghashshahum min al-yammi ma ghashshahum* (فَغَشّاهم مِنَ اليَمِّ ما غَشّاهم), with an alif in both places, a doubled *shin*, and the *ya'* omitted.

﴿And Pharaoh led his people astray﴾; that is, he called them to worship him. ﴿And did not guide﴾; that is, he did not guide them when he brought them to the watering places of destruction. This is a refutation of his statement: ﴿And I only guide you to the path of right conduct﴾ (Ghafir: 29).

﴿And We appointed for you the right side of the mount﴾ to receive the Torah. We mentioned the meaning of ﴿*al-ayman*﴾ in (Maryam: 52), and we mentioned ﴿the manna and the quails﴾ in (al-Baqarah: 57).

[﴿Eat﴾; that is, and We said to them: "Eat."]

﴿And do not transgress﴾: there are three opinions concerning this:
One: do not be insolent regarding My blessings [so that you wrong others].
The second: do not deny My blessings, so that you become transgressors.
The third: do not store any of it for more than a day and a night.

﴿Then My wrath will descend upon you﴾; that is, then My punishment will become binding upon you. Most readers read *fa-yahilla* (فَيَحِلَّ) with a *kasra* on the *ha'*, and *man yahlil* (ومَن يَحْلِلْ) with a *kasra* on the *lam*. Al-Kisa'i read *fa-yahullu* (فَيَحُلُّ) with a *damma* on the *ha'*, and *man yahlul* (ومَن يَحْلُلْ) with a *damma* on the *lam*. Al-Farra' said: the *kasra* is more beloved to me, because the *damma* derives from *hulul* ("alighting"), meaning "falling," whereas *yahilla* with a *kasra* means "becomes binding," and the explanation has come with "binding," not with "falling."

﴿Then he has fallen﴾; that is, he has perished.

﴿And indeed I am Forgiving﴾: *al-Ghaffar* is the One who forgives the sins of His servants again and again. Whenever their sins recur, His forgiveness recurs. The root of *al-ghafr* is "covering." From it the nap of a garment (*zi'bir al-thawb*, زِئْبِرُ الثَّوْبِ) is called *ghafr* (غَفْرًا), because it covers its warp. Thus *al-Ghaffar* is the One who covers the sins of His servants, and who draws over them the garment of His mercy.

﴿For those who repent﴾: Ibn 'Abbas said: for those who repent from *shirk*. ﴿And believe﴾; that is, who affirm God's oneness and believe in Him. ﴿And do righteous deeds﴾: who perform the obligatory duties.

Concerning His statement ﴿then remain guided﴾ there are eight opinions:
One: he knows that for this deed there is a reward. Abu Salih reported this from Ibn 'Abbas.
The second: he does not doubt. Ibn Abi Talha reported this from Ibn 'Abbas.
The third: he knows that this is success (*tawfiq*) from God [for him]. 'Ata' reported this from Ibn 'Abbas.
The fourth: he adheres to the Sunnah and the community (*al-jama'ah*). Said ibn Jubayr said this.
The fifth: he remains upright. Al-Dahhak said this.
The sixth: he adheres to Islam until he dies upon it. Qatada said this.
The seventh: he is guided in how to act. Zayd ibn Aslam said this.
The eighth: he is guided to the guardianship (*wilayah*) of the household of the Prophet (ﷺ). Thabit al-Bunani said this.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 20, verses 90–94:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And Harun had already said to them before this﴾; that is, before Musa came. ﴿O my people, you are only being tested by it﴾; that is, you are being tried. ﴿And indeed, your Lord is the Most Merciful﴾, not the calf. ﴿They said, "We will not cease to be devoted to it until Musa returns to us."﴾; that is, we will not stop remaining in the worship of the calf. ﴿When Musa returned﴾ [to them]. ﴿He said, "O Harun, what prevented you, when you saw them going astray,﴾ by worshipping the calf. ﴿That you did not follow me?"﴾ The reading of Ibn Kathir and Abu Amr is: ﴿Alla tattabi'ani﴾ with a sukun (silent) ya' in connected speech; Ibn Kathir pauses on the ya', while Abu Amr pauses without a ya'. Isma'il ibn Ja'far related from Nafi': ﴿Alla tattabi'aniya af'asaytа﴾ with a fathah on the ya'. Qalun related from Nafi' exactly like Abu Amr. ʿAsim, Ibn ʿAmir, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read it without a ya' in both connected speech and pause. The meaning is: what prevented you from following me? And "la" (lā) is an extra (zā'idah) word.

As for the meaning, there are three opinions:

The first: "You should follow behind me with those of the believers who are with you, and separate from them." This was related by Sa'id ibn Jubayr from Ibn ʿAbbas.

The second: "That you should fight them directly." This was related by Abu Salih from Ibn ʿAbbas.

The third: It is in the sense of rebuke against them. This was said by Muqatil.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Have you then disobeyed my command?﴾ This is His saying in the charge He gave him: ﴿Take my place among my people and act righteously﴾. The exegetes said: Then he seized his brother by the head and beard, out of anger at him. Although this is not mentioned here, it was mentioned in (al-A'raf: 150), so this was sufficient. We have explained there the meaning of ﴿O son of my mother﴾ and the differences of the readers concerning it.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Nor by my head﴾; that is, by the hair of my head. This anger was for the sake of Allah, mighty and majestic, not for his own self; because it occurred to him that Harun had disobeyed Allah by not following Musa.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, I feared﴾; that is, if I separated from them and followed you, ﴿that you would say, "You have caused division among the Children of Israel."﴾ And concerning this there are two opinions:

One: by my following you and those believers who are with me. The second: by my fighting some of them against others.

Regarding His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And you did not observe my word﴾ there are two opinions:

One: you did not observe my word to you: ﴿Take my place among my people and act righteously﴾.

The second: you did not await my command concerning them.

**Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on Surah 20, verses 95–98:**

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿What is your business, O Samiri?﴾ That is: what is your matter and your affair that led you to do what you did? Ibn al-Anbari said: Some linguists (lughawiyyun) say: *al-khatb* (affair, matter) is derived from *al-khitab* (address, speech). The meaning is: what is the matter about which you address (others)?

They differed over the name of the Samiri, in two views:

The first: he is also named Musa. This was said by Wahb ibn Munabbih, who said: he was the paternal cousin of Musa ibn Imran.

The second: he is Mikha. This was said by Ibn al-Sa'ib.

Was he from the Children of Israel or not? On this there are two views:

The first: he was not from them. This was said by Ibn Abbas.

The second: he was one of their leaders, and he was from a tribe called Samira. This was said by Qatada.

As for his country, there are two views:

The first: Kirman. This was said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr. The second: Bajarma. This was said by Wahb.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿I saw what they did not see﴾. Hamza and al-Kisa'i read *tabsurū* with a *ta'* (addressing everyone). According to the reading of the majority (al-jumhur), it refers to the Children of Israel; according to this reading, he addressed all of them. Abu Ubayda said: "I knew what you did not know." He said: Some people say: *basurtu* and *absartu* are the same, like *asra'tu* and *sara'tu*. Al-Zajjaj said: It is said: *basura al-rajulu yabsuru*, when he becomes knowledgeable about a thing, and *absara yubsiru*, when he looks. The exegetes (al-mufassirun) said: Musa said to him: "And what is that?" He said: "I saw Jibril on a horse, and it was cast into my soul that I should take a handful from its trace." ﴿So I took a handful﴾. Ubayy ibn Ka'b, al-Hasan, and Mu'adh al-Qari read *qabsatan* with a *sad*. Al-Farra' said: *al-qabdah* with the whole palm, and *al-qabsah* with the *sad*, with the tips of the fingers. Ibn Qutayba said: Similar to this are: *al-khadm* (eating) with the whole mouth and *al-qadm* with the tips of the teeth; *al-nadkh* is more than *al-nadh* (sprinkling); *al-rijz* is punishment, and *al-rijs* is filth; *al-hulas* is in the body and *al-sulas* in the mind; *al-ghalat* is an error in speech, and *al-ghalat* in calculation; *al-khasir* is one who feels cold, and *al-kharis* is one who feels cold and hunger; *al-nar al-khamidah* is the fire whose flame has subsided but whose embers have not been extinguished, and *al-hamidah* is that which has been extinguished and gone entirely; *al-shakd* is a gift given at the start, and if it is a reward, it is *shakm*; *al-ma'ih* is one who enters the well and fills the bucket, and *al-matih* is one who draws it up.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Then I threw it﴾; that is: I cast it into the calf. Abu 'Amr, Hamza, al-Kisa'i, and Khalaf read *fanabadhat-ha* with idgham (assimilation). ﴿And thus﴾; that is: and just as you were told, ﴿my soul enticed me﴾; that is: it made it attractive to me. ﴿He said﴾: Musa said, "Go"; that is: away from among us. ﴿For you, in this life﴾; that is: as long as you are alive, ﴿is to say: "No touching"﴾; that is: "I will not touch, and I will not be touched." So the Samiri began to wander in the wilderness with the wild animals and beasts, touching no one and no one touching him. God punished him with this, and inspired him to say: ﴿No touching﴾. Whenever he met anyone, he would say: "No touching," that is: do not come near me and do not touch me. This became a punishment for his offspring too, so that their remnants today, as the exegetes mentioned, in the land of al-Sham, say this. It is reported that if one of them touched someone from others, both would be seized by fever immediately.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And for you there is an appointment﴾; that is: for your punishment on the Day of Resurrection. ﴿You will not be able to escape it﴾; that is: it will not be delayed for you. Whoever pronounces the *lam* of *tukhlafahu* with a kasra means: you will not be absent from it.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Look at your god﴾, meaning the calf, ﴿to which you remained devoted﴾. Ibn Abbas said: its meaning is: you remained upon it. Al-Farra' said: the meaning of *zalta* is: you did it during the day. Ubayy ibn Ka'b, Abu al-Jawza', and Ibn Ya'mur read *zalta* with a *dhamma* on the *za'*. Ibn Mas'ud, Abu Raja', al-A'mash, and Ibn Abi Abla read *zilta* with a kasra on the *za'*. Al-Zajjaj said: *zalta* and *zilta* with a fatha and kasra on the *za'*. Whoever reads with a fatha, the original form is *zallaltа* (*ẓallaltа*), but the *lam* was dropped due to the heaviness of the doubling and the kasra, and the *za'* remained with its fatha. Whoever reads *zilta* with a kasra transfers the kasra of the *lam* onto the *za'*. The meaning of ﴿devoted﴾ (*'akifan*) is: staying/remaining. ﴿We will surely burn it﴾: the majority read *lanuharriqannahu* with a *dhamma* on the *nun*, a fatha on the *ha'*, and a shadda on the *ra'*. Ali ibn Abi Talib, Abu Razin, and Ibn Ya'mur read *lanahruqannahu* with a fatha on the *nun*, a sukun on the *ha'*, and a *raf'* on the *ra'* without doubling. Abu Hurayra, al-Hasan, and Qatada read *lanuhriqannahu* with a *raf'* on the *nun*, a sukun on the *ha'*, and a kasra on the *ra'* without doubling. Al-Zajjaj said: if it is doubled, the meaning is: we burn it time after time. The interpretation of ﴿we will surely burn it﴾ is: we will surely cool it down; it is said: *haraqtu ahraqu* and *ahriqu*, when I cooled the thing. *Al-nasf* is scattering (winnowing). It has come in the tafsir that Musa took the calf and slaughtered it, and blood flowed from it, because it had become flesh and blood. Then he burned it with fire, then scattered it into the sea. Then Musa informed them about their god, and said: ﴿Your god is only God, there is no god but Him﴾; that is: He is the one who deserves worship, not the calf. ﴿He encompasses all things in knowledge﴾; that is: His knowledge encompasses all things.

**Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on Surah 20, verses 95–98:**

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿What is your business, O Samiri?﴾ That is: what is your matter and your affair that led you to do what you did? Ibn al-Anbari said: Some linguists (lughawiyyun) say: *al-khatb* (affair, matter) is derived from *al-khitab* (address, speech). The meaning is: what is the matter about which you address (others)?

They differed over the name of the Samiri, in two views:

The first: he is also named Musa. This was said by Wahb ibn Munabbih, who said: he was the paternal cousin of Musa ibn Imran.

The second: he is Mikha. This was said by Ibn al-Sa'ib.

Was he from the Children of Israel or not? On this there are two views:

The first: he was not from them. This was said by Ibn Abbas.

The second: he was one of their leaders, and he was from a tribe called Samira. This was said by Qatada.

As for his country, there are two views:

The first: Kirman. This was said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr. The second: Bajarma. This was said by Wahb.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿I saw what they did not see﴾. Hamza and al-Kisa'i read *tabsurū* with a *ta'* (addressing everyone). According to the reading of the majority (al-jumhur), it refers to the Children of Israel; according to this reading, he addressed all of them. Abu Ubayda said: "I knew what you did not know." He said: Some people say: *basurtu* and *absartu* are the same, like *asra'tu* and *sara'tu*. Al-Zajjaj said: It is said: *basura al-rajulu yabsuru*, when he becomes knowledgeable about a thing, and *absara yubsiru*, when he looks. The exegetes (al-mufassirun) said: Musa said to him: "And what is that?" He said: "I saw Jibril on a horse, and it was cast into my soul that I should take a handful from its trace." ﴿So I took a handful﴾. Ubayy ibn Ka'b, al-Hasan, and Mu'adh al-Qari read *qabsatan* with a *sad*. Al-Farra' said: *al-qabdah* with the whole palm, and *al-qabsah* with the *sad*, with the tips of the fingers. Ibn Qutayba said: Similar to this are: *al-khadm* (eating) with the whole mouth and *al-qadm* with the tips of the teeth; *al-nadkh* is more than *al-nadh* (sprinkling); *al-rijz* is punishment, and *al-rijs* is filth; *al-hulas* is in the body and *al-sulas* in the mind; *al-ghalat* is an error in speech, and *al-ghalat* in calculation; *al-khasir* is one who feels cold, and *al-kharis* is one who feels cold and hunger; *al-nar al-khamidah* is the fire whose flame has subsided but whose embers have not been extinguished, and *al-hamidah* is that which has been extinguished and gone entirely; *al-shakd* is a gift given at the start, and if it is a reward, it is *shakm*; *al-ma'ih* is one who enters the well and fills the bucket, and *al-matih* is one who draws it up.

So the Samiri began to wander in the wilderness with the wild animals and beasts, touching no one and no one touching him. God punished him with this, and inspired him to say: ﴿No touching﴾. Whenever he met anyone, he would say: "No touching," that is: do not come near me and do not touch me. This became a punishment for his offspring too, so that their remnants today, as the exegetes mentioned, in the land of al-Sham, say this. It is reported that if one of them touched someone from others, both would be seized by fever immediately.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 20, verse 99–104:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Thus We relate to you﴾; that is: just as We have related to you, O Muhammad, the news of Musa and his people, We relate to you ﴿some of the news of what has passed before﴾; that is, some of the reports of those who came before. The "reminder" (adh-dhikr) here is the Qur'an. ﴿Whoever turns away from it﴾ by not believing in it and not acting upon what is in it, ﴿indeed, he will carry on the Day of Resurrection a burden (wizr)﴾. ʿIkrimah, Abu al-Mutawakkil, and ʿAsim al-Jahdari recited (yuhammalu) with a damma on the yaʾ, a fatha on the ḥaʾ, and a shadda on the mim. ﴿A burden﴾; that is, a sin. ﴿Abiding therein﴾; that is, in the punishment of that burden. ﴿And evil will it be for them﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is, "the burden will be evil for them ﴿on the Day of Resurrection as a load (ḥimlan)﴾," and ﴿ḥimlan﴾ is in the accusative as a specification (tamyiz).

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿The Day the Horn is blown﴾. Abu ʿAmr recited (nanfukhu) with a nun. The rest of the seven readers recited (yunfakhu) with a yaʾ, in the passive form (ʿala ma lam yusamma fa'iluh). Abu ʿImran al-Jawni recited (yawma yanfukhu) with a fathed yaʾ and a raised fa', and its explanation has already preceded. ﴿And We will gather the criminals﴾. Ubayy ibn Kaʿb, Abu al-Jawza', and Talhah ibn Musarrif recited (wa-yahshuru) with a fathed yaʾ and a raised shin. Ibn Masʿud, al-Hasan, and Abu ʿImran recited (wa-yuhsharu) with a raised yaʾ and a fathed shin, and (al-mujrimun) with a waw. The exegetes said: what is meant by "the criminals" is the polytheists. ﴿That Day, blue-eyed (zurqan)﴾. Concerning this there are two views:

One: blind, narrated by Abu Salih from Ibn ʿAbbas. Ibn Qutaybah said: white-eyed from blindness, the blackness and the pupil having gone.

The second: blue-eyed from the intensity of thirst, said by al-Zuhri. The meaning is that He disfigures their creation with blackened faces and blue eyes.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿They will whisper among themselves﴾; that is, some of them will speak secretly to others, ﴿You remained not but ten nights﴾; that is, you remained only ten nights. This is by way of minimizing, not as a precise limit.

Concerning the place intended by this stay there are two views:

One: the graves. Within this there are two views: one, that they meant the length of time they stayed in them. Abu Salih narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas: "If you remained after death but ten." The second: the period between the two blasts, which is forty years, for then the punishment is lightened for them, so they consider the duration of their stay small because of the terror of what they witness. This was related by ʿAli ibn Ahmad al-Nisaburi.

The second view: they meant their stay in this world, said by al-Hasan and Qatadah.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿When their best in course (amthaluhum tariqah) says: You remained not but a day﴾; that is, the most intelligent of them and the most just in speech, ﴿You remained not but a day﴾. So the people forgot the measure of their stay because of the terror of what they witnessed.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Thus We relate to you﴾; that is: just as We have related to you, O Muhammad, the news of Musa and his people, We relate to you ﴿some of the news of what has passed before﴾; that is, some of the reports of those who came before. The "reminder" (adh-dhikr) here is the Qur'an. ﴿Whoever turns away from it﴾ by not believing in it and not acting upon what is in it, ﴿indeed, he will carry on the Day of Resurrection a burden (wizr)﴾. ʿIkrimah, Abu al-Mutawakkil, and ʿAsim al-Jahdari recited (yuhammalu) with a damma on the yaʾ, a fatha on the ḥaʾ, and a shadda on the mim. ﴿A burden﴾; that is, a sin. ﴿Abiding therein﴾; that is, in the punishment of that burden. ﴿And evil will it be for them﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is, "the burden will be evil for them ﴿on the Day of Resurrection as a load (ḥimlan)﴾," and ﴿ḥimlan﴾ is in the accusative as a specification (tamyiz).

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿The Day the Horn is blown﴾. Abu ʿAmr recited (nanfukhu) with a nun. The rest of the seven readers recited (yunfakhu) with a yaʾ, in the passive form (ʿala ma lam yusamma fa'iluh). Abu ʿImran al-Jawni recited (yawma yanfukhu) with a fathed yaʾ and a raised fa', and its explanation has already preceded. ﴿And We will gather the criminals﴾. Ubayy ibn Kaʿb, Abu al-Jawza', and Talhah ibn Musarrif recited (wa-yahshuru) with a fathed yaʾ and a raised shin. Ibn Masʿud, al-Hasan, and Abu ʿImran recited (wa-yuhsharu) with a raised yaʾ and a fathed shin, and (al-mujrimun) with a waw. The exegetes said: what is meant by "the criminals" is the polytheists. ﴿That Day, blue-eyed (zurqan)﴾. Concerning this there are two views:

One: blind, narrated by Abu Salih from Ibn ʿAbbas. Ibn Qutaybah said: white-eyed from blindness, the blackness and the pupil having gone.

The second: blue-eyed from the intensity of thirst, said by al-Zuhri. The meaning is that He disfigures their creation with blackened faces and blue eyes.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿They will whisper among themselves﴾; that is, some of them will speak secretly to others, ﴿You remained not but ten nights﴾; that is, you remained only ten nights. This is by way of minimizing, not as a precise limit.

Concerning the place intended by this stay there are two views:

One: the graves. Within this there are two views: one, that they meant the length of time they stayed in them. Abu Salih narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas: "If you remained after death but ten." The second: the period between the two blasts, which is forty years, for then the punishment is lightened for them, so they consider the duration of their stay small because of the terror of what they witness. This was related by ʿAli ibn Ahmad al-Nisaburi.

The second view: they meant their stay in this world, said by al-Hasan and Qatadah.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿When their best in course (amthaluhum tariqah) says: You remained not but a day﴾; that is, the most intelligent of them and the most just in speech, ﴿You remained not but a day﴾. So the people forgot the measure of their stay because of the terror of what they witnessed.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 20, verses 105–114:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿They will ask you about the mountains﴾. The occasion of its revelation: "Some men from Thaqif came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: 'O Muhammad, what will the mountains be like on the Day of Resurrection?' So this verse was revealed." Abu Salih narrated it from Ibn Abbas.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿So say: My Lord will blow them away with a blast﴾. The commentators said: al-nasf (blowing away) is al-tadhriyah (scattering). The meaning: He will turn them into sand that flows like a flood, then turn them into carded wool, which the winds will carry off and uproot. ﴿And He will leave it﴾, i.e., He will leave their places in the earth after He has blown them away, ﴿a level plain﴾. Ibn Qutaybah said: al-qa' (level ground) of the earth is the flat land over which water stands, and al-safsaf is also flat; he means that there is no vegetation in it.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿You will not see in it any crookedness or unevenness﴾. On this there are three opinions:

One: that al-iwaj (crookedness) means valleys, and al-amt (unevenness) means elevations. This was narrated by Ibn Abi Talhah from Ibn Abbas. Likewise Mujahid said: al-iwaj is depression and al-amt is elevation. This is the view of al-Hasan. Ibn Qutaybah said: al-amt is al-nabk (hillocks).

The second: that al-iwaj is deviation and al-amt is a trace, like the strap of a sandal. This was narrated by al-Awfi from Ibn Abbas.

The third: that al-iwaj is a crack (fissure) and al-amt is a mound.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿On that Day they will follow the caller﴾. Al-Farra' said: i.e., they will follow the voice of the caller to the gathering; they have no deviation from his call; they cannot refrain from following.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And voices will be hushed﴾, i.e., they will be still and subdued, ﴿so you will hear nothing but a murmur﴾. On this there are three opinions:

One: the falling of footsteps. This was narrated by al-Awfi from Ibn Abbas, and al-Hasan, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Ikrimah, and Mujahid in one narration said so, and al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj chose it.

The second: the moving of lips without speech. This was narrated by Sa'id ibn Jubayr from Ibn Abbas.

The third: low speech. This was reported from Mujahid, and Abu Ubaydah said: a low sound.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿On that Day intercession will not benefit, except for one whom the Most Merciful has permitted, and whose word He approves﴾. It means: intercession will benefit no one, except the intercession of one whom the Most Merciful has permitted, i.e., permitted that he be interceded for; ﴿and whose word He approves﴾, i.e., He approves a word for the one interceded for, namely the one who in the world was among the people of "There is no god but Allah." ﴿He knows what is before them﴾: the pronoun refers to those who follow the caller. We have explained this verse in Surah al-Baqarah (2:255).

There are two opinions regarding the pronoun in ﴿with it﴾: One: it refers to Allah, the Exalted; this was said by Muqatil. The second: it refers to "what is before them and what is behind them"; this was said by Ibn al-Sa'ib.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And faces will be humbled﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: 'anat in the language means "submitted"; it is said: 'anā ya'nū, when he submitted. From this it is said: the lands were taken 'anwatan when they were taken by force, and taken with submission from their people. The commentators are of the view that this is on the Day of Resurrection, except what was narrated from Talq ibn Habib: it is placing the forehead and the nose, the two palms, the two knees, and the tips of the two feet on the ground for prostration. We have explained the meaning of ﴿the Living, the Self-Subsisting﴾ in the verse of the Throne (2:255).

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And he has indeed failed who carries an injustice﴾. Ibn Abbas said: he has lost who associated partners with Allah.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And whoever does righteous deeds while he is a believer﴾: the "min" here is for the genus. He stipulated faith because the deeds of a non-believer are not accepted and are not righteous. ﴿Then he will not fear﴾, i.e., he does not fear. Ibn Kathir recited ﴿fa-la yakhaf﴾ in the prohibitive form.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Injustice or diminishment﴾. On this there are four opinions:

One: he does not fear that he will be wronged by having his evil deeds increased, nor that he will be diminished in his good deeds. This was narrated by Ibn Abi Talhah from Ibn Abbas.

The second: he does not fear that he will be wronged by having the sin of others added to his, nor that his good deeds will be diminished. This was said by Qatadah.

The third: he does not fear being held accountable for what he did not do, nor having his righteous deed reduced. This was said by al-Dahhak.

The fourth: he does not fear that he will not be rewarded for his deed, nor that his due will be reduced. This was said by Ibn Zayd. The lexicographers said: al-hadm is reduction. The Arabs say: "I diminished for you from my right," i.e., I lowered. From it: so-and-so is hadim al-kashhayn, i.e., slender in the sides. And it is said: this is something that digests food, i.e., its weight reduces. Some commentators distinguished between injustice and diminishment, saying: injustice is withholding the whole right, and diminishment is withholding part of it, though that too is injustice.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And thus We have sent it down﴾, i.e., just as We have explained in this surah, ﴿We have sent it down﴾, i.e., We have sent down this Book, ﴿as an Arabic Qur'an, and We have repeated in it some of the warnings﴾, i.e., We have clarified in it various kinds of warning. Qatadah said: i.e., its accounts of the nations that denied.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿That perhaps they may fear Allah﴾, i.e., so that it may be a cause for their guarding against associating partners by taking warning from those before them. ﴿Or it causes them to remember﴾, i.e., the Qur'an renews for them; it was said: the warning. ﴿A reminder﴾, i.e., consideration, so that they may remember through it the punishment of the nations and take heed. Ibn Mas'ud and Asim al-Jahdari recited: ﴿aw nuhdith﴾ with a raised nun.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿So exalted is Allah﴾, i.e., He is far above the blasphemy of the blasphemers and the statements of the polytheists about His attributes. ﴿The King﴾ in whose hand is everything; ﴿the Truth﴾, which we have mentioned in (Yunus 10:32).

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And do not hasten with the Qur'an﴾. Regarding its occasion of revelation there are two opinions:

One: "Jibril used to come to the Prophet (ﷺ) with a surah and verses and recite them to him, and Jibril would not finish its end before the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) began speaking its beginning, fearing that he would forget it. So this verse was revealed." Abu Salih narrated it from Ibn Abbas.

The second: "A man slapped his wife, and she came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) seeking retaliation. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) set retaliation between them. Then this verse was revealed, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) paused until the saying of Allah, the Exalted, was revealed: ﴿Men are the protectors of women﴾ (4:34)." This was said by al-Hasan al-Basri.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Before its revelation to you is completed﴾. Ibn Mas'ud, al-Hasan, and Ya'qub recited nuqdi (with nun, kasra on the dad, and fatha on the ya'), and wahyahu (with a fatha on the ya').

There are three opinions regarding the meaning of the speech:

One: do not hasten in its recitation before Jibril finishes reciting it, fearing forgetting it; this is according to the first opinion.

The second: do not teach it to your companions until We explain its meanings to you; this was said by Mujahid and Qatadah.

The third: do not ask for its descent before the revelation comes to you; this was mentioned by al-Mawardi.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And say: My Lord, increase me in knowledge﴾. On this there are three opinions:

One: increase me in Qur'an; this was said by Muqatil. The second: understanding. The third: memorization. Al-Tha'labi mentioned both.

It means: intercession will benefit no one, except the intercession of one whom the Most Merciful has permitted, i.e., permitted that he be interceded for; ﴿and whose word He approves﴾, i.e., He approves a word for the one interceded for, namely the one who in the world was among the people of "There is no god but Allah." ﴿He knows what is before them﴾: the pronoun refers to those who follow the caller. We have explained this verse in Surah al-Baqarah (2:255).

There are two opinions regarding the pronoun in ﴿with it﴾: One: it refers to Allah, the Exalted; this was said by Muqatil. The second: it refers to "what is before them and what is behind them"; this was said by Ibn al-Sa'ib.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And faces will be humbled﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: 'anat in the language means "submitted"; it is said: 'anā ya'nū, when he submitted. From this it is said: the lands were taken 'anwatan when they were taken by force, and taken with submission from their people. The commentators are of the view that this is on the Day of Resurrection, except what was narrated from Talq ibn Habib: it is placing the forehead and the nose, the two palms, the two knees, and the tips of the two feet on the ground for prostration. We have explained the meaning of ﴿the Living, the Self-Subsisting﴾ in the verse of the Throne (2:255).

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And he has indeed failed who carries an injustice﴾. Ibn Abbas said: he has lost who associated partners with Allah.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And whoever does righteous deeds while he is a believer﴾: the "min" here is for the genus. He stipulated faith because the deeds of a non-believer are not accepted and are not righteous. ﴿Then he will not fear﴾, i.e., he does not fear. Ibn Kathir recited ﴿fa-la yakhaf﴾ in the prohibitive form.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Injustice or diminishment﴾. On this there are four opinions:

One: he does not fear that he will be wronged by having his evil deeds increased, nor that he will be diminished in his good deeds. This was narrated by Ibn Abi Talhah from Ibn Abbas.

The second: he does not fear that he will be wronged by having the sin of others added to his, nor that his good deeds will be diminished. This was said by Qatadah.

The third: he does not fear being held accountable for what he did not do, nor having his righteous deed reduced. This was said by al-Dahhak.

The fourth: he does not fear that he will not be rewarded for his deed, nor that his due will be reduced. This was said by Ibn Zayd. The lexicographers said: al-hadm is reduction. The Arabs say: "I diminished for you from my right," i.e., I lowered. From it: so-and-so is hadim al-kashhayn, i.e., slender in the sides. And it is said: this is something that digests food, i.e., its weight reduces. Some commentators distinguished between injustice and diminishment, saying: injustice is withholding the whole right, and diminishment is withholding part of it, though that too is injustice.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And thus We have sent it down﴾, i.e., just as We have explained in this surah, ﴿We have sent it down﴾, i.e., We have sent down this Book, ﴿as an Arabic Qur'an, and We have repeated in it some of the warnings﴾, i.e., We have clarified in it various kinds of warning. Qatadah said: i.e., its accounts of the nations that denied.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿That perhaps they may fear Allah﴾, i.e., so that it may be a cause for their guarding against associating partners by taking warning from those before them. ﴿Or it causes them to remember﴾, i.e., the Qur'an renews for them; it was said: the warning. ﴿A reminder﴾, i.e., consideration, so that they may remember through it the punishment of the nations and take heed. Ibn Mas'ud and Asim al-Jahdari recited: ﴿aw nuhdith﴾ with a raised nun.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿So exalted is Allah﴾, i.e., He is far above the blasphemy of the blasphemers and the statements of the polytheists about His attributes. ﴿The King﴾ in whose hand is everything; ﴿the Truth﴾, which we have mentioned in (Yunus 10:32).

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And do not hasten with the Qur'an﴾. Regarding its occasion of revelation there are two opinions:

One: "Jibril used to come to the Prophet (ﷺ) with a surah and verses and recite them to him, and Jibril would not finish its end before the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) began speaking its beginning, fearing that he would forget it. So this verse was revealed." Abu Salih narrated it from Ibn Abbas.

The second: "A man slapped his wife, and she came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) seeking retaliation. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) set retaliation between them. Then this verse was revealed, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) paused until the saying of Allah, the Exalted, was revealed: ﴿Men are the protectors of women﴾ (4:34)." This was said by al-Hasan al-Basri.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Before its revelation to you is completed﴾. Ibn Mas'ud, al-Hasan, and Ya'qub recited nuqdi (with nun, kasra on the dad, and fatha on the ya'), and wahyahu (with a fatha on the ya').

There are three opinions regarding the meaning of the speech:

One: do not hasten in its recitation before Jibril finishes reciting it, fearing forgetting it; this is according to the first opinion.

The second: do not teach it to your companions until We explain its meanings to you; this was said by Mujahid and Qatadah.

The third: do not ask for its descent before the revelation comes to you; this was mentioned by al-Mawardi.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And say: My Lord, increase me in knowledge﴾. On this there are three opinions:

One: increase me in Qur'an; this was said by Muqatil. The second: understanding. The third: memorization. Al-Tha'labi mentioned both.

[p. 328] The statement of the Exalted: ﴿And We had certainly made a covenant with Adam﴾; that is, We commanded him and charged him not to eat from the tree. ﴿Before﴾; that is, before these people who broke My covenant and abandoned faith in Me, whom He mentioned in His saying: ﴿so that they may be mindful﴾. The meaning is: if they broke the covenant, Adam too had been given a covenant, but he forgot.

Regarding this forgetting, there are two views:

The first: it means abandonment (al-tark), said by Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid. The meaning is that he abandoned what he had been commanded.

The second: it is forgetting in the sense opposed to remembrance (al-dhikr), related by al-Mawardi.

Mu'adh al-Qari', 'Asim al-Jahdari, and Ibn al-Sumayfa' read فَنُسِّيَ (fa-nussiya) with a raised nun and a shadda on the sin.

The statement of the Exalted: ﴿and We did not find in him resolve﴾. Resolve ('azm) in the language means settling the self upon an action. Regarding its meaning there are four views:

The first: We did not find in him preservation; this was related by al-'Awfi from Ibn 'Abbas. The meaning is that he did not preserve what he had been commanded.

The second: patience; said by Qatadah and Muqatil. The meaning is that he did not show patience regarding what he was forbidden.

The third: firmness; said by Ibn al-Sa'ib. Ibn al-Anbari said: this does not remove Adam from the people of firm resolve (ulu al-'azm); rather, he had no resolve only concerning the eating, and nothing more.

The fourth: resolve in returning to the sin; mentioned by al-Mawardi. What follows this has already been explained in [al-Baqarah: 34], up to the statement of the Exalted: ﴿so let him not expel you both from the Garden, and [you] will be distressed﴾. The commentators said: what is meant by it is the toil and hardship of this world, from the burden of tilling, sowing, kneading, baking, and other things. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: a red ox was sent down to Adam, and he would work with it and wipe the sweat from his brow; that is his distress. The scholars said: the meaning is "you both will be distressed," but He did not say "you both will be distressed" for two reasons:

The first: Adam is the one addressed, so it was sufficient to mention him, as in the verse ﴿one seated on the right and on the left﴾ [Qaf: 17]; this was said by al-Farra'.

The second: since Adam was the earner, the toil fell more heavily upon him; mentioned by al-Mawardi.

The statement of the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, it is for you that you will not hunger therein, nor be naked﴾. Ubayy ibn Ka'b read لا تُجاعَ ولا تُعَرى (la tujā'a wa la tu'arā), with a dammed ta' and an alif. ﴿And that you will not thirst therein﴾: Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, and Hafs from 'Asim read وَأنَّكَ (wa-annaka) with an open alif. Nafi' and Abu Bakr from 'Asim read وَإنَّكَ (wa-innaka) with a kasra on the alif. Abu 'Ali said: whoever opens it takes it as "that for you is that you will not hunger, and that for you is that you will not thirst"; whoever puts a kasra begins a new statement.

The statement of the Exalted: ﴿you will not thirst therein﴾; that is, you will not be parched. It is said: the man was thirsty (zami'a al-rajul zama'an), so he is thirsty ('atshan), meaning parched. The phrase "la tadhha" ("you will not be exposed to the sun") means: you will not be exposed to the sun so that its heat strikes you, for there is no sun in the Garden.

The statement of the Exalted: ﴿Shall I direct you to the tree of eternity﴾; that is, to a tree whoever eats from it will not die, ﴿and a kingdom that does not decay﴾; its new state does not wear out and does not perish. What follows this has been explained in [al-A'raf: 22].

Regarding the statement of the Exalted: ﴿and he disobeyed﴾, there are two views:

The first: he lost the path to eternity, since he sought it before the disobedience.

The second: his life became corrupt for him, because the meaning of ghayy (error) is corruption. Ibn al-Anbari said: some of the commentators erred and said the meaning of ﴿ghawa﴾ is that he ate too much from the tree until he was overfull and surfeited, as it is said: the young camel ghawa when it drinks too much of its mother's milk and becomes surfeited, nearly dying. This is wrong for two reasons: [p. 330]

The first: it is not said from surfeit "ghawa yaghwi"; rather it is said "ghawiya yaghwa."

The second: the statement of the Exalted: ﴿When they tasted the tree﴾ [al-A'raf: 22] indicates that they had not eaten excessively, nor was the punishment delayed from them until they reached excess. Ibn Qutaybah said: we say about Adam: "he disobeyed and erred," as Allah the Mighty and Majestic said, but we do not say "Adam is a disobedient one and an erring one," just as you would say of a man who cut his cloth and sewed it: "he has cut it and sewed it," but you do not say "this is a tailor," until he repeatedly does that action and is known for it.

The statement of the Exalted: ﴿Then his Lord chose him﴾. We have already explained choosing (al-ijtiba') in [al-An'am: 87]. ﴿So He accepted his repentance and guided him﴾; that is, He guided him to repentance. ﴿He said: Go down﴾. Regarding those addressed by it, there are two views:

The first: Adam and Iblis; said by Muqatil.

The second: Adam and Eve; said by Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi. The meaning of the statement of the Exalted: ﴿some of you are enemies to others﴾ is Adam and his offspring, Iblis and his offspring, and the serpent as well. We have explained this in [al-Baqarah: 36].

The statement of the Exalted: ﴿Whoever follows My guidance﴾; that is, My messenger and My Book, ﴿will not go astray, nor will he be distressed﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: whoever recites the Qur'an and follows what is in it, Allah will guide him from error and protect him from the evil of reckoning. Allah has guaranteed for whoever follows the Qur'an that he will not go astray in this world and will not be distressed in the Hereafter. Then he recited this verse.

The statement of the Exalted: ﴿But whoever turns away from My remembrance﴾. 'Ata' said: from My admonition. Ibn al-Sa'ib said: from the Qur'an, and he did not believe in it, nor follow it.

The statement of the Exalted: ﴿then indeed for him is a constricted life﴾. Abu 'Ubaydah said: its meaning is a narrow life. The word ḍankun (constricted) is applied to the feminine and the masculine without a ta' marbuta; and every life, or place, or dwelling that is narrow is ḍankun. He recited:

"And if they dwell in a constriction, then dwell [with them]."

Al-Zajjaj said: the root meaning of ḍankun in the language is narrowness and hardship.

The commentators have five views regarding what is meant by this life:

The first: it is the punishment of the grave. Abu Hurayrah narrated from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that he said: "Do you know what the constricted life is?" They said: "Allah and His Messenger know best." He said: "It is the punishment of the disbeliever in his grave. By Him in whose hand my soul is, ninety-nine serpents (tinnin) will be set upon him, blowing into his body, stinging him and scratching him until the Day of Resurrection." Among those who held that it is the punishment of the grave were Ibn Mas'ud, Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, and al-Suddi.

The second: it is the squeezing of the grave until his ribs interlock; narrated by 'Ata' from Ibn 'Abbas.

The third: it is the hardship of his life in the Fire; narrated by al-Dahhak from Ibn 'Abbas, and held by al-Hasan, Qatadah, and Ibn Zayd. Ibn al-Sa'ib said: that life is of ḍarī' (a thorny plant) and zaqqum (a tree of Hell).

The fourth: the constricted life is earnings from what is unlawful; narrated by al-Dahhak from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: the constricted life is that the doors of good are closed to him, so he is not guided to any of them, and he has an unlawful livelihood in which he rushes about. Al-Dahhak said: this livelihood is the wicked earning, and 'Ikrimah held the same view.

The fifth: the constricted life is wealth whose owner does not fear Allah concerning it; narrated by al-Awfi from Ibn 'Abbas.

Thus three views emerge regarding the place of the life: the first, the grave; the second, this world; the third, Hell.

Regarding the statement of the Exalted: ﴿and We will raise him on the Day of Resurrection blind﴾. Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir, and Hafs from 'Asim read أَعْمى (a'mā) and حَشَرْتَنِي أَعْمى (ḥashartanī a'mā) with open mims. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, and Abu Bakr from 'Asim read them with kasra on both. Nafi' read between the kasra and the fatha. Then regarding this blindness, the commentators have two views:

The first: blindness of sight; Abu Salih narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: when he is brought out of the grave he comes out seeing, but when he is driven to the place of gathering he becomes blind.

The second: blind to the proof; said by Mujahid and Abu Salih. Al-Zajjaj said: its meaning is that he has no proof by which he may be guided, because people have no proof against Allah after the messengers.

The statement of the Exalted: ﴿Thus﴾; that is, the matter is as you see, ﴿Our signs came to you, but you forgot them﴾; that is, you abandoned them and did not believe in them, and just as you abandoned them in the world, so you are abandoned today in the Fire. ﴿And thus﴾; that is, as We have mentioned, ﴿We recompense whoever transgresses﴾; that is, whoever associates partners with Allah, ﴿and the punishment of the Hereafter is more severe﴾ than the punishment of this world and than the punishment of the grave, ﴿and more lasting﴾, because it endures.
