Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 20, verse 128–130:

The Almighty's saying: ﴿Has it not guided them?﴾ That is: has it not become clear to the disbelievers of Makkah, when they look at the traces of the peoples whom We destroyed? The Quraysh used to trade, and they would see the dwellings of ʿĀd and Thamūd, in which were signs of destruction. This is the meaning of His saying: ﴿walking among their dwellings﴾. Zayd narrated from Yaʿqūb: (Afa-lam nahdi) with a nūn.

The Almighty's saying: ﴿And had it not been for a word that preceded from your Lord﴾ regarding the deferral of the punishment from these disbelievers until the Day of Resurrection. It was also said: until the Day of Badr; and it was said: until the end of their terms. ﴿It would have been inevitable (lizāman)﴾; that is, the punishment would have been inevitable (lāziman), i.e., binding upon them. Lizām is a verbal noun (maṣdar) used as a description of the punishment. Al-Farrāʾ and Ibn Qutaybah said: in this verse there is inversion (taqdīm wa-taʾkhīr), and the meaning is: and had it not been for a word and a specified term, it would have been inevitable.

The Almighty's saying: ﴿So be patient over what they say﴾. God Almighty commanded His Prophet to be patient over the harm he hears from them, until God judges concerning them. Then He judged concerning them with killing, and by the verse of the sword (āyat al-sayf) the unrestricted command to be patient was abrogated (naskh, abrogation: the cancelling of a previous ruling by a later one).

The Almighty's saying: ﴿And glorify with the praise of your Lord﴾; that is, pray to Him with praise of Him and extolling of Him, ﴿before the rising of the sun﴾, meaning the dawn (Fajr) prayer, ﴿and before its setting﴾, meaning the ʿAṣr prayer, ﴿and during the hours of the night﴾. Ānāʾ (hours) means the periods of time; we have explained it in (Āl ʿImrān: 113). ﴿Then glorify﴾; that is, then pray.

Regarding the intended meaning of this prayer there are four opinions:

The first: the Maghrib and the ʿIshāʾ prayers. This was narrated by Abū Ṣāliḥ from Ibn ʿAbbās, and Qatādah said likewise.

The second: the middle of the night, narrated by al-ʿAwfī from Ibn ʿAbbās. (p-334)

The third: the ʿIshāʾ prayer, said by Mujāhid and Ibn Zayd.

The fourth: the beginning, middle and end of the night, said by al-Ḥasan.

The Almighty's saying: ﴿And the extremities of the day﴾. The meaning: and glorify the extremities of the day. Al-Farrāʾ said: they are only two extremities, but they came in the form of the plural, like His saying: ﴿If you two turn to God, your hearts have indeed inclined﴾ [al-Taḥrīm: 4].

Among the exegetes, regarding the intended meaning of this prayer there are three opinions:

The first: that it is the Ẓuhr prayer, said by Qatādah. According to this, the Ẓuhr prayer was called "the extremities of the day" because its time begins at the zenith (zawāl), so it is the end of the first half and the beginning of the second half.

The second: that it is the Maghrib prayer and the Ṣubḥ prayer, said by Ibn Zayd. This is on the basis that Fajr is at the beginning of the first extremity and Maghrib at the end of the second extremity.

The third: that they are Fajr, Ẓuhr and ʿAṣr; according to this, Fajr is from the first extremity, and Ẓuhr and ʿAṣr are from the second extremity, as related by al-Farrāʾ.

The Almighty's saying: ﴿So that you may be pleased﴾. Ibn Kathīr, Nāfiʿ, Abū ʿAmr, Ibn ʿĀmir, Ḥamzah, and Ḥafṣ from ʿĀṣim read (tarḍā) with a fatḥah on the tā'. Al-Kisāʾī and Abū Bakr from ʿĀṣim read it with a ḍammah. As for the one who reads it with a fatḥah, the meaning is: so that you may be pleased with the reward of God which He gives you. As for the one who reads it with a ḍammah, there are two aspects:

One of them: so that you may be pleased with what you are given. The second: that God may be pleased with you.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 20, verse 128–130:

The Almighty's saying: ﴿Has it not guided them?﴾ That is: has it not become clear to the disbelievers of Makkah, when they look at the traces of the peoples whom We destroyed? The Quraysh used to trade, and they would see the dwellings of ʿĀd and Thamūd, in which were signs of destruction. This is the meaning of His saying: ﴿walking among their dwellings﴾. Zayd narrated from Yaʿqūb: (Afa-lam nahdi) with a nūn.

The Almighty's saying: ﴿And had it not been for a word that preceded from your Lord﴾ regarding the deferral of the punishment from these disbelievers until the Day of Resurrection. It was also said: until the Day of Badr; and it was said: until the end of their terms. ﴿It would have been inevitable (lizāman)﴾; that is, the punishment would have been inevitable (lāziman), i.e., binding upon them. Lizām is a verbal noun (maṣdar) used as a description of the punishment. Al-Farrāʾ and Ibn Qutaybah said: in this verse there is inversion (taqdīm wa-taʾkhīr), and the meaning is: and had it not been for a word and a specified term, it would have been inevitable.

Then He judged concerning them with killing, and by the verse of the sword (āyat al-sayf) the unrestricted command to be patient was abrogated (naskh, abrogation: the cancelling of a previous ruling by a later one).

Ānāʾ (hours) means the periods of time; we have explained it in (Āl ʿImrān: 113). ﴿Then glorify﴾; that is, then pray.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 20, verses 131–132:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And do not extend your eyes toward that by which We have provided pairs of them, the splendor of the worldly life, that We may test them therein.﴾ Its occasion of revelation is what Abu Rafi', the freed slave of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), narrated, saying: "A guest arrived at the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he called me and sent me to a man of the Jews who sold food, saying: 'Tell him: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) says: "Sell me such-and-such measure of flour, or lend it to me until the crescent of Rajab."' So I went to him and told him that. The Jew said: 'By Allah, I will not sell it to him nor lend it except against a pledge.' So I came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and informed him. He said: 'By Allah, if he had sold it to me or lent it to me, I would have repaid it. Indeed I am trustworthy in the heavens and trustworthy on the earth. Go with my iron coat of mail to him.'" And this verse was revealed as a consolation to him concerning the world."

Ubayy ibn Ka'b said: Whoever is not consoled by the consolation of Allah, his soul will be consumed by regrets over the world.

The tafsir of this verse has already passed at the end of (Surah) al-Hijr (15:88).

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿the splendor of the worldly life﴾. Ibn Mas'ud, al-Hasan, al-Zuhri and Ya'qub read (zahrata) with a fatha on the ha'. Al-Zajjaj said: It is in the accusative by the sense of (matta'na) ("We gave enjoyment"), because the meaning of (matta'na) is: We made for them the worldly life a splendor. ﴿That We may test them therein﴾; i.e., that We make that a trial for them. Ibn Qutaybah said: that We may examine them. The exegetes said: The splendor of the world is its brightness and freshness, and what pleases the beholder when he sees it, and it is from the blossom of plants and their beauty.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿But the provision of your Lord is better and more lasting﴾. Concerning it there are two opinions:

One: that it is His reward in the Hereafter. Two: contentment.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And enjoin prayer upon your family﴾. The exegetes said: What is meant by "his family" is his people and those who follow his religion, and the people of his household enter into this.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And be steadfast in it﴾; i.e., be patient in prayer. ﴿We do not ask you for provision﴾ (p-336); i.e., We do not burden you with providing for yourself or for Our creation; rather We command you to worship, and your provision is upon Us. ﴿And the good outcome is for piety﴾; i.e., the good end is for the people of piety. Bakr ibn Abdullah al-Muzani, whenever his family was in want, would say: "Get up and pray," then he would say: "With this Allah and His Messenger commanded," and he would recite this verse.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 20, verse 133–135:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And they say﴾ — meaning the polytheists — ﴿"Why does he not bring us a sign from his Lord?"﴾ — that is, why does Muhammad not bring us signs like those of the prophets, such as the she-camel and the staff. ﴿Has there not come to them﴾ — Nafi', Abu 'Amr, and Hafs on the authority of 'Asim read (ta'tihim) with a ta' (feminine). Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, and Abu Bakr on the authority of 'Asim read (ya'tihim) with a ya' (masculine).

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿clear evidence of what is in the former scriptures?﴾ — that is, has there not come to them in the Qur'an a clarification of what is in the books concerning the reports of the nations whom We destroyed when they asked for signs and then disbelieved in them? So what assures them that their situation in asking for signs is not like the situation of those (nations)? ﴿And if We had destroyed them﴾ — meaning the polytheists of Makkah — ﴿with a punishment before it﴾ — regarding the pronoun (ha') there are two views:

One: it refers to the Book (the Qur'an), said by Muqatil. The second: it refers to the Messenger, said by al-Farra'.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿they would have said﴾ on the Day of Resurrection, ﴿"Our Lord, why did You not send to us a messenger,﴾ — that is, why not? — ﴿so that we might follow Your signs﴾ — that is, act according to their requirements — ﴿before we were humiliated﴾ (p-337) by the punishment, ﴿and disgraced﴾ in Hell. Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn as-Sumaifa', and Abu Hatim on the authority of Ya'qub read (nudhilla wa-nukhza) with a damma on the nun in both and a fatha on the dhal. ﴿Say﴾ to them, O Muhammad: ﴿"Each﴾ of us and you ﴿is waiting;﴾ — that is, we await for you the punishment in this world, and you await for us the turns of fortune — ﴿so wait;﴾ — that is, await — ﴿and you will soon know﴾ when the command of Allah comes ﴿who are the companions of the even path,﴾ — that is, the upright religion — ﴿and who has been guided﴾ from error: is it we or you?" It has been said: this verse is abrogated by the verse of the sword, but this is not correct.
